(p-٣) Sūrat Banī Isrā'īl

Section on its revelation

It is Meccan according to the consensus (qawl al-jamā'a), except that some say it contains a Medinan portion. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbās that he said: "It is Meccan except for eight verses, from His saying: ﴿And indeed they were about to tempt you﴾ to His saying: ﴿a helper﴾ [al-Isrā' 73–75]." This is also the view of Qatādah. Muqātil said: Among its Medinan parts are: ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance﴾ [al-Isrā' 80]; His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge before it﴾ [al-Isrā' 107]; His saying: ﴿Indeed, your Lord encompasses the people﴾ [al-Isrā' 60]; His saying: ﴿And indeed they were about to tempt you﴾ [al-Isrā' 73]; His saying: ﴿And indeed they were about to drive you out﴾ [al-Isrā' 76]; and His saying: ﴿And had We not made you firm﴾ and what follows it [al-Isrā' 74, 75].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Glory be to Him﴾. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he was asked about the explanation of "Subḥān Allāh" (Glory be to God), and he said: "It is the declaration of God's transcendence above every imperfection." We have already mentioned this meaning in (al-Baqarah: 32). (p-٤)

Al-Zajjāj said: "Asrā" means "to make his servant travel," and it is said: "asraytu" and "saraytu" when I traveled by night. Both dialects have come in the Qur'an. God Most High said: ﴿By the night when it passes [yasri]﴾ [al-Fajr: 4].

Regarding the meaning of glorification here, there are two views:

The first: The Arabs glorify God (tasbīḥ) at the occurrence of something astonishing, as if God, Most High, is amazing His servants by the blessing He bestowed upon His Messenger.

The second: It came as a response to them, since when he told them about the Night Journey, they denied it. So the meaning is: God is far above taking a lying messenger.

There is no disagreement that the intended "His servant" here is Muḥammad (ﷺ).

Regarding His saying: ﴿from the Sacred Mosque﴾ there are two views:

The first: He was taken on the Night Journey from the very Mosque itself. This was said by al-Ḥasan and Qatādah, and it is supported by the ḥadīth of Mālik ibn Ṣa'ṣa'ah, which is in the two Ṣaḥīḥs: "While I was in al-Ḥaṭīm..." and some narrators sometimes said: "in al-Ḥijr."

The second: He was taken on the Night Journey from the house of Umm Hāni', and this is the view of most exegetes (mufassirūn). (p-٥) According to this view, "the Sacred Mosque" means the Ḥaram. The whole Ḥaram is a mosque, as mentioned by al-Qāḍī Abū Ya'lā and others.

As for ﴿the farthest mosque﴾: it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It was called "al-Aqṣā" (the farthest) because of the distance between the two mosques. The meaning of ﴿whose surroundings We have blessed﴾ is that God made rivers flow around it and caused fruits to grow. It is also said: because it is the abode of the prophets and the descent place of the angels.

The scholars differed over whether he entered Bayt al-Maqdis or not. Abū Hurayrah narrated that he entered Bayt al-Maqdis, prayed there with the prophets, and then was taken up to the heavens. Ḥudhayfah ibn al-Yamān said: He did not enter Bayt al-Maqdis, nor pray in it, and did not descend from al-Burāq until he was taken up.

If it is said: What is the meaning of His saying ﴿to the farthest mosque﴾, when you say he ascended to the heavens?

The answer: The Night Journey was to that place, and the Ascension (mi'rāj) was from that place.

It is also said: The wisdom in mentioning this is that if he had been told of his ascent to the heavens at the beginning of the account, their denial would have been intense. When he was told about Bayt al-Maqdis, and his truthfulness in what he told them of the true signs became clear to them, he was then informed of his ascension.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That We may show him of Our signs﴾, meaning: what he saw, that is, the wonders of that night which he told the people about. ﴿Indeed, He is the Hearing﴾ of the statements of Quraysh, ﴿the Seeing﴾ of them. We have mentioned the ḥadīths of the Ascension in our book entitled "al-Ḥadā'iq," and we disliked prolonging it here.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verses 2–3:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave Moses the Book﴾. When in the previous verse He mentioned the honour of Muhammad (ﷺ), in this one He mentioned the dignity of Moses. The "Book" is the Torah (al-Tawrat).

﴿And We made it a guidance for the Children of Israel﴾; that is, We guided them by it to the right path. ﴿That you not take﴾: Abu 'Amr read it as (yattakhidhu) with the letter ya', and the meaning is: We guided them so that they would not take. The rest read it with the letter ta', and Abu 'Ali said: it is a shift from the third person to the second person after the absence, like: ﴿Praise be to Allah﴾, then He said: ﴿You alone do we worship﴾.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿a Guardian (wakilan)﴾. Mujahid said: a partner. Al-Zajjaj said: a lord. Ibn al-Anbari said: the Lord is called Wakil only because of His sufficiency and His standing over the affairs of His servants; for the wakil among people is known to attend to the affairs of those who depend on him and to look after their matters, so the Lord is a wakil in this respect, not in the sense of raising the station of the one who appoints or lowering the status of the one who acts as agent.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the offspring of those whom We carried﴾. Mujahid said: it is a vocative, "O offspring of those whom We carried." Ibn al-Anbari said: whoever reads (que tattakhidhu) with the ta', then after "offspring" there is an implied element that has been omitted, relying on what precedes it as evidence; its summary is: "O offspring of those whom We carried with Noah, do not take a guardian." It is also permissible to dispense with the implied element by His saying: ﴿Indeed he was a grateful servant﴾, because it means: "Be thankful to Me as he was thankful." Whoever reads (ya-yattakhidhu) with the ya', makes the vocative connected to the address, and "offspring" is in the accusative by the vocative; it is also permissible to make it the object of "taking" as a second object, the summary of the speech being: that they not take the offspring of those whom We carried with Noah as a guardian. Qatada said: all of mankind are the offspring of those whom Allah saved in that ark.

The scholars said: the aspect of the blessing upon creation in this statement is that they were in the loins of those who were saved.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed he was a grateful servant﴾. Salman al-Farisi said: when he ate he would say, "Praise be to Allah," and when he drank he would say, "Praise be to Allah." Others said: when he put on a garment he would say, "Praise be to Allah," so Allah named him a grateful servant.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 4–6:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel﴾, there are two opinions regarding it:

The first: "We informed them." This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas.

The second: "We decreed against them." This was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, and Qatadah also said this. According to the first, "ila" remains in its original meaning, and the Book is the Torah. According to the second, "ila" carries the meaning of "ala" (upon/against), and the Book is the first Remembrance.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿You will surely cause corruption on earth﴾, meaning: the land of Egypt, ﴿twice﴾ through sins and opposition to the Torah.

Regarding those among the prophets whom they killed in the first corruption, there are two opinions:

The first: Zechariah, said by al-Suddi from his shaykhs.

The second: Sh'ya (Isaiah), said by Ibn Ishaq. As for the prophet killed in the second corruption, he is Yahya ibn Zakariyya (John the Baptist). Muqatil said: between the two corruptions was two hundred and ten years.

As for the reason for their killing of Zechariah: they accused him concerning Maryam, saying, "She conceived from him." So he fled from them, and a tree split open for him, and he entered it, but a piece of his cloak remained outside. Then Satan came to them and pointed them to him, and they cut the tree with a saw while he was in it. As for the reason for their killing Sh'ya, it is that he stood among them with a message from God forbidding them from sins. It was also said: he is the one who fled from them and entered the tree until they cut it with the saw, and that Zechariah died of natural death.

As for the reason for their killing Yahya ibn Zakariyya, there are two opinions:

The first: that their king wished to marry a woman who was not lawful for him, and Yahya forbade him from her. Then there are four sayings concerning her: the first is that she was his brother's daughter, said by Ibn Abbas. The second is that she was his daughter, said by Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr. The third is that she was his brother's wife, and that was not permissible among them, said by al-Husayn ibn Ali, peace be upon them both. The fourth is that she was the daughter of his wife, said by al-Suddi from his shaykhs, and he mentioned that the reason for this was: the king of the Children of Israel desired his wife's daughter, so he asked Yahya about marrying her, and he forbade him. So her mother became enraged with Yahya when he forbade him from marrying her daughter. She set about adorning her daughter and sent her to the king when he sat at his drinking, and commanded her to pour for him and to present herself to him; if he wanted her for herself, she should refuse until the head of Yahya ibn Zakariyya is brought in a basin. She did so, and he said, "Woe to you, ask me for anything other than this." She said, "I want nothing but this." So he gave the order, and his head was brought, and the head was speaking, saying, "It is not lawful for you, it is not lawful for you."

The second opinion: that the king's wife saw Yahya, peace be upon him, and he had been given beauty and comeliness, so she desired him for herself, but he refused. So she said to her daughter, "Ask your father for the head of Yahya," and he gave her what she asked. This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas. The scholars of history said: the blood of Yahya kept boiling until seventy thousand of the Children of Israel were killed over it, and then it calmed. It was also said: it did not calm until his killer came and said, "I killed him," and he was killed, and then it calmed.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you will surely become exceedingly haughty﴾; that is, you will be arrogant toward obedience and will transgress.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So when the promise of the first of them came﴾; that is, the punishment of the first of the two times, ﴿We sent upon you servants of Ours﴾; that is, We dispatched against you, and there are five opinions concerning them:

The first: they are Goliath (Jalut) and his soldiers, said by Ibn Abbas and Qatadah. The second: Bukhtansar (Nebuchadnezzar), said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, and preferred by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. The third: the Amalekites, who were disbelievers, said by al-Hasan. The fourth: Sennacherib, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The fifth: a people from the people of Persia, said by Mujahid. Ibn Zayd said: God gave power over them to Sabur Dhu al-Aktaf of the kings of Persia.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿possessing great might﴾; that is, possessors of numbers and strength in fighting.

Concerning His saying: ﴿and they went through the houses﴾ there are three opinions:

The first: they walked between their dwellings, said by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas. Mujahid said: they searched out their news, and there was no fighting. al-Zajjaj said: they roamed through the houses looking to see whether anyone remained whom they had not killed. And "al-jaws" means seeking a thing with thoroughness.

The second: they killed them among their houses, said by al-Farra' and Abu Ubayda.

The third: they spread corruption and wrought havoc; it is said "jasu" and "hasu," so they "yajusuna" and "yahusuna" when they do that, said by Ibn Qutaybah.

As for "khilal": it is the plural of "khilal," which is the space between two things. Abu Razin, al-Hasan, Ibn Jubayr, and Abu al-Mutawakkil read "khalal al-diyar" with a fatha on the kha and the lam, without an alif. ﴿And it was a promise to be fulfilled﴾; that is, there is no avoiding its occurrence.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then We gave you the return of victory over them﴾; that is, We granted you victory over them. The meaning of "karrah" is return and turn of fortune, and that was when Dawud killed Jalut and their kingdom returned to them. al-Farra' related that a man invoked against Bukhtansar, so God destroyed him and their kingdom returned to them. It was also said: they raided the king of Babylon and took what was in his hand of wealth and captives.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We made you more in number as supporters﴾; that is, more in number and helpers than them. Ibn Qutaybah said: "nafir" and "nafir" are one and the same, as one says "qadir" and "qadir," and its origin is: one who goes forth with a man from his clan and the people of his household.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then We gave you the return of victory over them﴾; that is, We granted you victory over them. The meaning of "karrah" is return and turn of fortune, and that was when Dawud killed Jalut and their kingdom returned to them. al-Farra' related that a man invoked against Bukhtansar, so God destroyed him and their kingdom returned to them. It was also said: they raided the king of Babylon and took what was in his hand of wealth and captives.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We made you more in number as supporters﴾; that is, more in number and helpers than them. Ibn Qutaybah said: "nafir" and "nafir" are one and the same, as one says "qadir" and "qadir," and its origin is: one who goes forth with a man from his clan and the people of his household.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verses 7–8:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If you do good﴾; that is, and We said to you: if you do good, by obeying Allah, ﴿you do good for yourselves﴾; that is, the outcome of obedience is for you. ﴿And if you do evil﴾ through corruption and sins, ﴿then it is against themselves﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

One of them: it means "then to it" (ilayha). The second: "then against it" (alayha).

﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter comes﴾, the response to "fa-idha" is omitted; its estimated meaning is: so when the promise of the punishment of the second time, for your corruption, comes, We sent them so that they would disgrace your faces. This second corruption was their killing of Yahya ibn Zakariyya (Yahya, son of Zechariah), and their intention to kill ʿIsa (Jesus), but he was raised up; and Allah gave power over them to the kings of Persia and the Romans, who killed them and took them captive. That is His saying: ﴿to disgrace your faces﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu ʿAmr, and Hafs from ʿAsim recited (li-yasu'u) with a yā' (ya) on the plural and with a hamza between the two waws, the reference being to those who were sent. Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza, and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim recited (li-yasu'a wujuhakum) in the singular. Abu ʿAli said: in it there are two possibilities: one, that it refers to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, "so that Allah may disgrace"; the second, that it refers to the sending (al-ba'th), "so that the sending may disgrace." Al-Kisa'i recited (linasu'a) with a nun, which refers back to Allah Exalted.

Regarding who was sent against them in the second time there are two opinions:

One of them: Bukhtanassar (Nebuchadnezzar), said by Mujahid and Qatadah. Many of the narrators reject this opinion, saying that there was a long period between the destruction of Bukhtanassar of Bayt al-Maqdis and the birth of Yahya ibn Zakariyya.

The second: Antiochus the Roman (Anṭiyākhus al-Rūmī), said by Muqatil. The meaning of ﴿to disgrace your faces﴾ is: so that they bring grief upon you by what they do of killing you and taking you captive. Disgrace was specifically attributed to the faces, and what is meant is the people themselves, because the effect of grief and dejection appears upon them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and that they may enter the Masjid﴾, meaning: Bayt al-Maqdis, ﴿as they entered it﴾ the first time, ﴿and that they may destroy what they have conquered﴾; that is, that they may ruin and devastate. Al-Zajjaj said: tibr is said of anything that breaks of glass, iron, or gold; and the meaning of ﴿what they have conquered﴾ is: that they may destroy while they are in a position of dominance over you.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you﴾. This is among what they were promised in the Torah. "It may be" (ʿasa) from Allah is binding, so Allah had mercy on them after His vengeance upon them, restored their lands, and returned their blessings after seventy years. ﴿And if you return﴾ to Our disobedience, ﴿We return﴾ to punishing you. The exegetes said: then they returned to disobedience, so Allah sent against them kings from the kings of Persia and the Romans. Qatadah said: then the last of that was that Allah sent against them Muhammad ﷺ, so they are in punishment until the Day of Resurrection, giving the jizya from willing submission while they are humbled.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have made Hell for the disbelievers a prison﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

One of them: a prison, said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Dahhak, and Qatadah. Mujahid said: they will be confined therein. Abu ʿUbayda and Ibn Qutaybah said: a place of confinement. Al-Zajjaj said: "ḥaṣīran" means confinement, taken from your saying "ḥaṣartu al-rajul" (I confined the man) when I imprisoned him, so he is "maḥṣūr" (confined), and this is his ḥaṣīr, i.e., his place of confinement. The ḥaṣīr is also woven matting, named so because its strands are confined (ḥuṣirat) together, and the ribs of the chest are called ḥaṣīr because some of the ribs are confined with others. Ibn al-Anbari said: ḥaṣīran means ḥāṣiratan (enclosing), changed from ḥāṣira to ḥaṣīr, just as "mu'lim" was changed to "alīm".

The second: a bed and a cushion, said by al-Hasan. Abu ʿUbayda said: it is also possible that Hell is for them a bed like the ḥaṣīr, and the ḥaṣīr is a small rug.

That is because the believers were suffering harm from the polytheists, so God hastened for them the good tidings in this world by the punishment of the disbelievers.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 11:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And man prays for evil as he prays for good﴾. This is because man, in a state of impatience and anger, calls down upon himself and his family things he would not want to be answered, just as he prays for good for himself. ﴿And man has ever been hasty﴾: he hastens in invoking evil in anger and impatience just as he hastens in invoking good.

Regarding the intended meaning of "man" (al-insan) here, there are three opinions:

The first: it is a generic noun (ism jins) by which people in general are meant. This was said by al-Zajjaj and others.

The second: it is Adam, and the singular is used in place of his descendants. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

The third: it is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, when he said: ﴿So rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal: 32]. This was said by Muqatil. Salman al-Farisi said: The first thing Allah created of Adam was his head, and he began to look at his body as it was being created. He said: "Then his two legs remained, so he said: 'My Lord, hasten [their creation].'" That is His saying: ﴿And man has ever been hasty﴾.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 12:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We made the night and the day two signs﴾; that is, two indicators showing the power of their Creator. ﴿Then We effaced the sign of the night﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

One of them: the sign of the night is the moon, and its effacement is the darkness that is in some part of the moon. This meaning was held by ʿAlī, peace be upon him, and Ibn ʿAbbās, along with others.

The second: the sign of the night was effaced by the darkness that was made to accompany the night, so the effacing was attributed to the darkness since it erases and nullifies lights. This was related by Ibn al-Anbārī. It is also narrated that the sun and the moon were equal in light and brightness, so God sent Gabriel, who passed his wing over the face of the moon and obliterated its light.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We made the sign of the day﴾, meaning the sun, ﴿visible﴾ (mubṣira). Concerning this there are three opinions:

The first: "luminous" (munīra), said by Qatādah. Ibn al-Anbārī said: the describing of the sign as "seeing" (ibṣār) is appropriate only in a figurative sense, as one says: "Time has played with the sons of so-and-so."

The second: the meaning of "mubṣira" is "giving sight by it" (mubaṣṣiran bihā), said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The third: the meaning of "mubṣira" is "making things seen" (mubaṣṣira), so the form mufʿil takes the place of mufaʿʿil, and the meaning is that it makes people see, that is, it shows them things; said by Ibn al-Anbārī. The meanings of the opinions are close to one another.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That you may seek bounty from your Lord﴾; that is, that you may see how you conduct your affairs and seek your provision by day. ﴿And that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾, through the effacing of the sign of the night; were it not for that, the night would not be distinguished from the day, and the number would not be made clear. ﴿And everything﴾, that is, whatever they need, ﴿We have detailed in detail﴾, that is, We have made it clear with a clarity by which it is not confused with anything else.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 13–14:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And every person⁠—⁠﴾. Ibn Abi ʿAbla recited (wa-kullu) with a raised lam (wa-kullu-un). Ibn Masʿud, Ubayy and al-Hasan recited (alzamnahu ṭayrahu) with a silent yaʾ and without an alif.

Regarding the ṭair (ṭāʾir, "bird"; here meaning fate or lot), there are four opinions.

The first: it is his wretchedness and his happiness. This was said by Abu Salih, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas. Mujahid said: "No child is born except that on his neck is a scroll on which is written whether he is wretched or happy."

The second: it is his deed. This was said by al-Farraʾ, and from al-Hasan there are two similar opinions.

The third: it is what befalls him. This was said by Khusayf. Abu ʿUbayda said: it is his portion (ḥaẓẓ).

Ibn Qutayba said: "The meaning, as I see it, and God knows best, is that every person has a portion of good and evil which God has decreed for him [upon him], so it is fixed to his neck. The Arabs say of everything that clings to a person: 'It has clung to his neck,' and 'This is upon me and around my neck until I come out of it.' The portion of good and evil was called ṭāʾir ('bird') because of the Arabs' saying: 'The bird has run for him with such-and-such good,' and 'The bird has run for him with such-and-such evil,' in the manner of omen and augury. So God addressed them in terms they use, and informed them that the matter which they attribute to the bird is what clings to their necks."

Al-Azhari said: "The origin of this is that when God, exalted is He, created Adam, He knew the obedient among his descendants and the disobedient, so He wrote down what He knew of them all, and decreed happiness for whom He knew to be obedient and wretchedness for whom He knew to be disobedient. Thus each of them has that to which he will return at the time of his creation and origination. That is His saying: ﴿We have fixed his bird to his neck﴾."

The fourth: it is what is taken as an omen from the like of a deed he did. The mention of the neck is an expression for its being bound to him, like a necklace clinging to the neck among what is worn. This is the saying of al-Zajjaj. Ibn al-Anbari said: the origin of their calling the deed a ṭāʾir is that they used to take omens from some deeds.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We bring forth for him﴾. Abu Jaʿfar recited (wa-yukhraju) with a raised yaʾ and a fatha on the rāʾ. Yaʿqub and ʿAbd al-Warith recited with a fatha on the yaʾ and a damma on the rāʾ. Qatada and Abu al-Mutawakkil recited (wa-yukhriju) with a raised yaʾ and a kasra on the rāʾ. Abu al-Jawzaʾ and al-Aʿraj recited (wa-takhruju) with a fatha on the tāʾ and a raised rāʾ. ﴿on the Day of Resurrection, a book﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿIkrima and al-Dahhak recited (kitābun) with a raise, "yalqāhu". Ibn ʿAmir and Abu Jaʿfar recited (yulaqqāhu) with a damma on the yaʾ and a shadda on the qāf. Hamza and al-Kisa'i inclined the qāf. The exegetes said: this is his book, in which is what he did. When Abu al-Sawwar al-ʿAdawi recited this verse he would say: "Two spreadings and a folding. As for while you live, O son of Adam, your scroll is spread out, so write in it what you wish; when you die it is folded; then when you are raised up it is spread out."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Read your book﴾. Abu Jaʿfar recited (iqraʾ) with the hamza lightened, and in it there is an implied element; its implied form is: "It will be said to him: Read your book." al-Hasan said: "He will read it, whether he was illiterate or not, and indeed He has been just to you in making you your own reckoner."

Regarding the meaning of ﴿a reckoner﴾ (ḥasīban) there are three opinions:

The first: one who calls to account. The second: a witness. The third: sufficient. The meaning is that the person is entrusted with his own reckoning, so that he knows God's justice among the servants, sees the necessity of God's proof against him and his deserving of punishment, and knows that if he enters Paradise it is by God's bounty and not by his deed, and if he enters the Fire it is by his sin. Ibn al-Anbari said: He said "ḥasīban" though nafs is feminine, because by nafs He means the person, or because the word nafs has no sign of feminine gender, so it was likened to "sky" and "earth." God, exalted is He, said: ﴿the sky splitting thereby﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 18]. The poet said:

"[Then no cloud poured its rain] nor land whose herbage grew green by its rain."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 15:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever is guided, is only guided for his own soul﴾; that is, he has the reward of his guidance, and upon him is the punishment of his misguidance.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾; that is, no burdened soul. ﴿The burden of another﴾. Ibn Abbas said: Al-Walid ibn al-Mughira said, "Follow me, and I will bear your burdens." So Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾. Abu Ubayda said: the meaning is, "a sinner will not bear the sin of another sinner." Al-Zajjaj said: it is said, "wazara, yazir, fa huwa wazir, wizran, wuzran, wazratan," and its meaning is: he sinned, a sin.

There are two interpretations of this verse:

The first: that the sinner is not seized for the sin of another.

The second: that a person should not act upon sin, because another has done it, just as the disbelievers said: ﴿Indeed, we found our fathers upon a community﴾ [Az-Zukhruf: 22]. The meaning of ﴿until We send a messenger﴾ is: until We make clear what it is that We punish for, and what it is on account of which We admit to Paradise.

Section

Qadi Abu Ya'la said: In this is evidence that knowledge of Allah is not obligatory by reason; rather it is obligatory by the Shari'a, which is the sending of the messengers, and that if a person died before that, it would not be decided that he is in the Fire. He said: It was also said: its meaning is that one is not punished in matters whose path is revelation (al-sam') except by the establishment of the proof of revelation through the Messenger. For this reason they said: if some of the people of the enemy territory (ahl al-harb) embrace Islam in the territory of war and have not heard of the prayer, zakat and the like, it is not obligatory on them to make up any of them, because they were not obligated except after the establishment of the proof of revelation. The basis for this is the case of the people of Quba when they turned toward the Ka'ba and did not restart. If someone embraces Islam in the territory of Islam and does not know of the obligation of prayer, then it is obligatory upon him to make up (the prayer), because he has seen people praying in the mosques with the adhan and iqama, and that is a summons to it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 16–17:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when We intend to destroy a town﴾. Regarding the cause of His intending this, there are two views:

One: what was already decreed for them in His judgment of wretchedness. The second: their obstinacy toward the prophets and their denial of them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We command its affluent ones﴾. Most readers recited "amarna" (أمرنا) with a light (unshaddened) mim, on the pattern of "fa'alna" (فعلنا), and regarding it there are three views:

The first: that it derives from the command (al-amr), and there is an ellipsis in the speech, its estimated sense being: "We commanded its affluent ones to obedience, so they transgressed." This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Al-Zajjaj said: a similar usage in speech is "I commanded you, so you disobeyed me," for it is known that disobedience is opposing a command.

The second: it means "We multiplied" (kaththarna). It is said: "amartu al-shay'" and "amartuhu" meaning "I multiplied it," and from this comes the expression "a mare that is ma'mura," meaning one with many offspring. It is said: "the sons of so-and-so amiru (أمروا) yaʼmuruna amran" when they became numerous. This is the statement of Abu 'Ubayda and Ibn Qutayba.

The third: that the meaning of "amarna" is "amrina" (we made [them] rulers): it is said "amartu al-rajul," meaning "I made the man a ruler," and the sense is: "We empowered its affluent ones with rule." Ibn al-Anbari mentioned this. Kharija related from Nafi': "a'marna" (آمرنا) with a long alif, like "a'mana," and Hammad ibn Salama related similarly from Ibn Kathir. This is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-Darda', Abu Razin, al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, and Ya'qub. Ibn Qutayba said: it is the well-known, prevalent dialect, and its meaning is also "we multiplied." Ibn Mujahid related that Abu 'Amr recited "ammarna" (أمّرنا) with a shaddah on the mim, and this is the narration of Aban from 'Asim; it is the reading of Abu al-'Aliya, al-Nakha'i, and al-Jahdari. Ibn Qutayba said: the meaning is: "We made them amirs (leaders)." And Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu al-Jawza', and Ibn Ya'mar recited "amirna" (أمِرنا) with a fatha on the hamza, a kasra on the mim, and light (unshaddened).

As for "al-mutrafun" (the affluent ones), they are the pampered who have been made insolent by blessings and ease of living. The exegetes say they are the tyrants, the powerful, and the kings. He singled out the affluent for mention only because they are the leaders, and whoever else is a follower of them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿so they committed wickedness therein﴾; that is, they rebelled in their disbelief, for wickedness in disbelief is going out to its most heinous extreme. We have explained the meaning of fisq (wickedness) in (al-Baqara: 26, 197).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿so the word became due against it﴾. Muqatil said: the punishment became obligatory upon it. We have mentioned the meaning of "destruction" (tadmir) in (al-A'raf: 137).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And how many generations have We destroyed﴾. It is the plural of qarn (generation). We have mentioned the differences of people regarding it in (al-An'am: 6), and we explained the meanings of "All-Knowing" (al-Khabir) and "All-Seeing" (al-Basir) in (al-Baqara). Muqatil said: this verse is a warning to the people of Makkah.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 18–19:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever desires the hastening (world)﴾ means: whoever directs his deeds toward the worldly life. He expressed the noun by means of the adjective. ﴿We hasten for him therein what We will﴾ of the goods of this world. It was also said: of expansion and restriction (of provision). ﴿For whom We will﴾ has two interpretations:

One of them: for whom We will to destroy him. This was said by Abu Ishaq al-Fazari.

The second: for whom We will to hasten something for him. In this there is a reproach of the one who directs his deeds toward the worldly life, and a clarification that he does not attain, together with what he seeks from it, except what has been decreed for him, and then he enters the Fire in the Hereafter. Ibn Jarir said: this verse concerns the one who does not believe with certainty in the Return. We have already mentioned the meaning of "Jahannam" (Hell) in (al-Baqarah: 206), the meaning of ﴿yaslaha﴾ (will burn in it) in (al-Nisa: 10), and the meaning of ﴿madhmuman madhhuran﴾ (blameworthy and rejected) in (al-A'raf: 18).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter﴾ means: the Garden. ﴿And strives for it with its striving﴾; that is, he performs for it the deed that is suitable for it. He said ﴿and he is a believer﴾ because faith is a condition for the validity of deeds. ﴿Then those, their striving will be appreciated﴾; that is, accepted. And the Exalted God's appreciation (shukr) for them is His reward to them and His praise of them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 20–22:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿To each — these and those — We extend﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "kullan" is in the accusative governed by "numiddu" (We extend), and "ha'ula'" is a substitute (badal) for "kull". The meaning is: We extend to these and to those from the bounty of your Lord. The commentators said: We give to each from the world, the righteous and the wicked alike. The "bounty" here is provision (rizq), and "mahzur" means "that which is withheld." The meaning is that provision encompasses both the believer and the disbeliever, while the Hereafter is for the God-conscious alone. ﴿Look﴾, O Muhammad, ﴿how We have favoured some of them over others﴾. There are two opinions regarding what they have been favoured in:

One: provision, some of them having little and some having much.

The second: provision and deeds, so that some of them are granted success in righteous deeds, and some of them are prevented from that.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Do not set up with Allah another god, lest you sit reproached and forsaken﴾. The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), while the meaning is general for all the responsible people. "Makhdhul" is the one who has no helper, and "khudhlan" is abandoning help. Muqatil said: It was revealed when they invited the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to the religion of his forefathers.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 23–25:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾. Ibn Abi Talha narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "It means: your Lord has commanded." Al-Dahhak transmitted from him that he said: "It is actually (wa-wassa rabbuka), so one of the two waws joined with the ṣad," and thus Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Abu al-Mutawakkil and Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited: (wa-wassa), "and has enjoined." This is contrary to what the consensus (ijma', the scholarly agreement on a matter) has settled upon, so it is not to be given any attention. Abu 'Imran, 'Asim al-Jahdari and Mu'adh al-Qari recited: (wa-qada'u rabbika), with a qaf and a dad, with a long vowel (madd), a hamza, the nominative on the word "qada'" and the genitive on the name "Rabb." Ibn al-Anbari said: "This qada' is of the category of certainty and obligation, but it is of the category of command and obligation. The root meaning of qada' in the language is: cutting a thing off with firmness and perfection." The poet said, lamenting 'Umar:

"I decided affairs, then I left after them calamities within their sheaths not yet split open."

He meant: I cut them off, making them firm.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And to the two parents, good treatment﴾; that is: and He commanded good treatment toward the two parents, which is kindness and honour. We have mentioned this in (al-Baqarah: 83).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If one of them or both reach old age with you﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir recited: (yablughanna), in the singular. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf recited: (yablughani), in the dual. Al-Farra' said: "(yablughanna) was made a verb for one of them, and 'kilahuma' (both) refers back to them both." Whoever recited (yuballighani), made it dual, because the two parents have been mentioned before this, so the verb matched their number. Then He said, "one of them or both," as a resumption, like His saying: ﴿So they were blind and deaf﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 71], then He resumed and said: ﴿many of them﴾.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So do not say to them "uff"﴾. Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr from 'Asim recited: (uffin) with a kasra and without tanwin. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Ya'qub and al-Mufaddal recited: (uffa) with a fatha and without tanwin. Nafi' and Hafs from 'Asim recited: (uffin) with a kasra and with tanwin. Abu al-Jawza' and Ibn Ya'mur recited: (uffun) with a damma and with tanwin and with shadda on the fa'. Mu'adh al-Qari, 'Asim al-Jahdari and Hamid ibn Qays recited: (uffan), like (ta'isan). Abu 'Imran al-Jawni and Abu al-Sammak al-'Adawi recited: (uffu) with a damma, without tanwin, with shadda on the fa', and this is the transmission of al-Asma'i from Abu 'Amr. 'Ikrimah, Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu Raja' and Abu al-Jawza' recited: (uff) with the fa' sukun and lightened; al-Akhfash said: "This is because some Arabs say '(uff laka)' by way of quotation, and the damma is ugly, because nothing with a lam came after it." Abu al-'Aliyah and Abu Husayn al-Asadi recited: (uffi) with shadda on the fa' and a ya'. Ibn al-Anbari transmitted that some recited it as (iffin) with a kasra on the hamza. Al-Zajjaj said: "In it there are seven dialect forms: the kasra without tanwin and with tanwin, the damma without tanwin and with tanwin, the fatha without tanwin and with tanwin, and the seventh dialect is not permissible in recitation: (uffi) with a ya', thus said al-Zajjaj." Ibn al-Anbari said: "In (uff) there are ten aspects: (uffa laka) with a fatha on the fa', (uffi) with a kasra, (uffu), (uffan laka) with the accusative and tanwin on the principle of supplication, as you say (waylan) for the disbelievers; (uffun laka) with the nominative and tanwin, and it is nominative by the lam, like His saying: ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 1]; (uffahin laka) with the genitive and tanwin, assimilated to sounds, like your saying (sahin, wamahin); (uffahan laka), also on the principle of supplication; (uffi laka) as an idafah to the self; (uff laka) with the fa' sukun, assimilated to particles, like (kam, hal, bal); and (iff laka) with a kasra on the alif." I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur the lexicographer, and he said: "You say: (uffi minhu), (uffa), (uffu), (uffin), (uffan), (uffin), (uffi) as an idafah, (uffaha), and (uffa) with an alif." Do not say (uffi) with a ya', for that is an error.

As for the meaning of (uff), there are five sayings:

The first: it is the filth of the fingernail, said by al-Khalil. The second: the filth of the ear, said by al-Asma'i. The third: the paring of the fingernail, said by Tha'lab. The fourth: that (al-uff) is contempt and belittling, from (al-affaf), and al-affaf among the Arabs is paucity, mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. The fifth: that (al-uff) is what you lift from the ground of a stick or reed, related by Ibn Faris the lexicographer. I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur, and he said: The meaning of (uff) is stench and irritation; its origin is your blowing on a thing that falls on you of dust and ash, and you want to remove the harm from it, so it is said of everything burdensome.

The author said: As for their saying (tuff), some people have taken it to mean (uff). It is narrated from Abu 'Ubayd that he said: The origin of (uff) and (tuff) is the dirt on the fingers when you twist it. Ibn al-Anbari related a distinction, saying: The lexicographers said: the origin of (uff) in the language is ear dirt, and (tuff) is fingernail dirt, and the Arabs used both for what is disliked, loathed and wearisome. Al-Zajjaj related another distinction, saying: It has been said that (uff) is fingernail dirt, and (tuff) is a trivial thing, like ear dirt, or a splinter taken from the ground; the meaning of (uff) is stench. The meaning of the verse: do not say to them a word by which you express irritation at them when they grow old and advanced in years; rather, you should take on from their service the same as what they undertook in caring for you and serving you. ﴿And do not reproach them﴾; that is: do not speak to them in irritation, shouting in their faces. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: do not shake your hand at them. It is said: nahartuhu anharuhu nahran, and intarahtuhu intiharan, with one meaning. Ibn Faris said: nahartu al-rajul and intarahtuhu, like zajartuhu. The exegetes said: He only forbade harming them in old age, though it is forbidden in every state, because in the state of old age there appears from them what irritates and harms, and their need for service increases.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And speak to them a noble word﴾; that is: a gentle, kind word, the best you can find. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: it is the word of a sinful slave to a harsh master.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾; that is: lower your side to them, humbling yourself before them out of your mercy toward them. The lowering of the wing has been explained in (al-Hijr: 88). 'Ata' said: "Your wing is your hands, so do not raise them over your parents." The majority pronounce the dhal of (al-dhull) with a damma. Abu Razin, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, 'Asim al-Jahdari and Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited it with a kasra on the dhal. Al-Farra' said: (al-dhull), with a damma, means that you humble yourself before them, from humiliation (dhull); and (al-dhull) with a kasra means that you humble yourself while not being humbled in service; (al-dhull) and (al-dhillah) are verbal nouns of (dhalil), and (al-dhull) with a kasra is the verbal noun of (dhalul), like (al-dabbah) and (al-ard). Ibn al-Anbari said: whoever recited (al-dhilla) with a kasra on the dhal made it mean (al-dhull) with a damma on the dhal. What the senior lexicographers hold is that (al-dhull) said of a man means the humble one, and (al-dhull) said of an animal means the tame one.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And say: "My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me when I was small"﴾; that is: like their mercy toward me in my childhood until they raised me. Some people held that this unrestricted supplication was abrogated regarding supplication for the people of polytheism by His saying: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 113]. This view is transmitted from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah and Muqatil. The author said: I do not regard this as abrogation according to the jurists, because it is a general ruling into which specification has entered, and Ibn Jarir has mentioned something close to what I have said.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Your Lord is most knowing of what is in your souls﴾; that is: of what you conceal of righteousness and disobedience. Whoever lets slip a hasty word while not harboring disobedience, will be forgiven for it, and this is His saying: ﴿If you are righteous﴾; that is: obedient to God [and it was said]: dutiful, and it was said: repentant. ﴿Indeed He is ever forgiving to the returners﴾. Regarding al-awwabin there are ten sayings:

The first: that it is the Muslim, narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas.

The second: that it is the one who repents repeatedly, narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, and Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and Abu 'Ubaydah said likewise. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is the one who repents again and again. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the penitent who desists from all that God has forbidden him, from (aba yauhu auban), meaning he returned.

The third: that it is the one who glorifies God (al-musabbih), narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: that it is the one who obeys God, the Exalted, narrated by 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas.

The fifth: that it is the one who mentions his sin in private and then seeks God's forgiveness for it, said by 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr.

The sixth: that it is the one who turns to God, the Exalted, with his heart and deeds, said by al-Hasan.

The seventh: the one who prays, said by Qatadah.

The eighth: the one who prays between Maghrib and 'Isha', said by Ibn al-Munkadir.

The ninth: the one who performs the Duha prayer, said by 'Awn al-'Uqayli.

The tenth: that it is the one who sins secretly and repents secretly, said by al-Suddi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If one of them or both reach old age with you﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir recited: (yablughanna), in the singular. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf recited: (yablughani), in the dual. Al-Farra' said: "(yablughanna) was made a verb for one of them, and 'kilahuma' (both) refers back to them both." Whoever recited (yuballighani), made it dual, because the two parents have been mentioned before this, so the verb matched their number. Then He said, "one of them or both," as a resumption, like His saying: ﴿So they were blind and deaf﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 71], then He resumed and said: ﴿many of them﴾.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So do not say to them "uff"﴾. Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr from 'Asim recited: (uffin) with a kasra and without tanwin. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Ya'qub and al-Mufaddal recited: (uffa) with a fatha and without tanwin. Nafi' and Hafs from 'Asim recited: (uffin) with a kasra and with tanwin. Abu al-Jawza' and Ibn Ya'mur recited: (uffun) with a damma and with tanwin and with shadda on the fa'. Mu'adh al-Qari, 'Asim al-Jahdari and Hamid ibn Qays recited: (uffan), like (ta'isan). Abu 'Imran al-Jawni and Abu al-Sammak al-'Adawi recited: (uffu) with a damma, without tanwin, with shadda on the fa', and this is the transmission of al-Asma'i from Abu 'Amr. 'Ikrimah, Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu Raja' and Abu al-Jawza' recited: (uff) with the fa' sukun and lightened; al-Akhfash said: "This is because some Arabs say '(uff laka)' by way of quotation, and the damma is ugly, because nothing with a lam came after it." Abu al-'Aliyah and Abu Husayn al-Asadi recited: (uffi) with shadda on the fa' and a ya'. Ibn al-Anbari transmitted that some recited it as (iffin) with a kasra on the hamza. Al-Zajjaj said: "In it there are seven dialect forms: the kasra without tanwin and with tanwin, the damma without tanwin and with tanwin, the fatha without tanwin and with tanwin, and the seventh dialect is not permissible in recitation: (uffi) with a ya', thus said al-Zajjaj." Ibn al-Anbari said: "In (uff) there are ten aspects: (uffa laka) with a fatha on the fa', (uffi) with a kasra, (uffu), (uffan laka) with the accusative and tanwin on the principle of supplication, as you say (waylan) for the disbelievers; (uffun laka) with the nominative and tanwin, and it is nominative by the lam, like His saying: ﴿Woe to the defrauders﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 1]; (uffahin laka) with the genitive and tanwin, assimilated to sounds, like your saying (sahin, wamahin); (uffahan laka), also on the principle of supplication; (uffi laka) as an idafah to the self; (uff laka) with the fa' sukun, assimilated to particles, like (kam, hal, bal); and (iff laka) with a kasra on the alif." I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur the lexicographer, and he said: "You say: (uffi minhu), (uffa), (uffu), (uffin), (uffan), (uffin), (uffi) as an idafah, (uffaha), and (uffa) with an alif." Do not say (uffi) with a ya', for that is an error.

As for the meaning of (uff), there are five sayings:

The first: it is the filth of the fingernail, said by al-Khalil. The second: the filth of the ear, said by al-Asma'i. The third: the paring of the fingernail, said by Tha'lab. The fourth: that (al-uff) is contempt and belittling, from (al-affaf), and al-affaf among the Arabs is paucity, mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. The fifth: that (al-uff) is what you lift from the ground of a stick or reed, related by Ibn Faris the lexicographer. I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur, and he said: The meaning of (uff) is stench and irritation; its origin is your blowing on a thing that falls on you of dust and ash, and you want to remove the harm from it, so it is said of everything burdensome.

The author said: As for their saying (tuff), some people have taken it to mean (uff). It is narrated from Abu 'Ubayd that he said: The origin of (uff) and (tuff) is the dirt on the fingers when you twist it. Ibn al-Anbari related a distinction, saying: The lexicographers said: the origin of (uff) in the language is ear dirt, and (tuff) is fingernail dirt, and the Arabs used both for what is disliked, loathed and wearisome. Al-Zajjaj related another distinction, saying: It has been said that (uff) is fingernail dirt, and (tuff) is a trivial thing, like ear dirt, or a splinter taken from the ground; the meaning of (uff) is stench. The meaning of the verse: do not say to them a word by which you express irritation at them when they grow old and advanced in years; rather, you should take on from their service the same as what they undertook in caring for you and serving you. ﴿And do not reproach them﴾; that is: do not speak to them in irritation, shouting in their faces. 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah said: do not shake your hand at them. It is said: nahartuhu anharuhu nahran, and intarahtuhu intiharan, with one meaning. Ibn Faris said: nahartu al-rajul and intarahtuhu, like zajartuhu. The exegetes said: He only forbade harming them in old age, though it is forbidden in every state, because in the state of old age there appears from them what irritates and harms, and their need for service increases.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And speak to them a noble word﴾; that is: a gentle, kind word, the best you can find. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: it is the word of a sinful slave to a harsh master.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾; that is: lower your side to them, humbling yourself before them out of your mercy toward them. The lowering of the wing has been explained in (al-Hijr: 88). 'Ata' said: "Your wing is your hands, so do not raise them over your parents." The majority pronounce the dhal of (al-dhull) with a damma. Abu Razin, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, 'Asim al-Jahdari and Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited it with a kasra on the dhal. Al-Farra' said: (al-dhull), with a damma, means that you humble yourself before them, from humiliation (dhull); and (al-dhull) with a kasra means that you humble yourself while not being humbled in service; (al-dhull) and (al-dhillah) are verbal nouns of (dhalil), and (al-dhull) with a kasra is the verbal noun of (dhalul), like (al-dabbah) and (al-ard). Ibn al-Anbari said: whoever recited (al-dhilla) with a kasra on the dhal made it mean (al-dhull) with a damma on the dhal. What the senior lexicographers hold is that (al-dhull) said of a man means the humble one, and (al-dhull) said of an animal means the tame one.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And say: "My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me when I was small"﴾; that is: like their mercy toward me in my childhood until they raised me. Some people held that this unrestricted supplication was abrogated regarding supplication for the people of polytheism by His saying: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 113]. This view is transmitted from Ibn Abbas, al-Hasan, 'Ikrimah and Muqatil. The author said: I do not regard this as abrogation according to the jurists, because it is a general ruling into which specification has entered, and Ibn Jarir has mentioned something close to what I have said.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Your Lord is most knowing of what is in your souls﴾; that is: of what you conceal of righteousness and disobedience. Whoever lets slip a hasty word while not harboring disobedience, will be forgiven for it, and this is His saying: ﴿If you are righteous﴾; that is: obedient to God [and it was said]: dutiful, and it was said: repentant. ﴿Indeed He is ever forgiving to the returners﴾. Regarding al-awwabin there are ten sayings:

The first: that it is the Muslim, narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas.

The second: that it is the one who repents repeatedly, narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas, and Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Dahhak and Abu 'Ubaydah said likewise. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is the one who repents again and again. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the penitent who desists from all that God has forbidden him, from (aba yauhu auban), meaning he returned.

The third: that it is the one who glorifies God (al-musabbih), narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: that it is the one who obeys God, the Exalted, narrated by 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas.

The fifth: that it is the one who mentions his sin in private and then seeks God's forgiveness for it, said by 'Ubayd ibn 'Umayr.

The sixth: that it is the one who turns to God, the Exalted, with his heart and deeds, said by al-Hasan.

The seventh: the one who prays, said by Qatadah.

The eighth: the one who prays between Maghrib and 'Isha', said by Ibn al-Munkadir.

The ninth: the one who performs the Duha prayer, said by 'Awn al-'Uqayli.

The tenth: that it is the one who sins secretly and repents secretly, said by al-Suddi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 26–28:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And give the near of kin his right﴾. There are two opinions regarding this:

The first: that it refers to the kinship of a man through his father and his mother. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Hasan. On this view, there are three opinions regarding their right: The first is that what is meant by it is showing them kindness (birr) and maintaining ties with them (silah). The second is the obligatory maintenance (nafaqah) due to them at the time of need. The third is a bequest (wasiyyah) to them at the time of death.

The second: that they are the near of kin of the Messenger, ﷺ. This is the view of ʿAli ibn al-Husayn, peace be upon them both, and al-Suddi. On this view, their right is giving them a share of the khums (one-fifth), and the address is to the rulers (al-wulat).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the needy and the wayfarer﴾. Abu Yaʿla al-Qadi said: It is permissible that what is meant is the obligatory charities (al-sadaqat al-wajibah), that is, the zakah; and it is permissible that it is the right which he is obliged to give when there is need for it. It has also been said: the right of the needy is from charity, and the wayfarer's is from hospitality (al-diyafah).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not squander wastefully﴾. Regarding squandering (tabdhir) there are two opinions:

The first: that it is spending wealth in what is not right. This was said by Ibn Masʿud and Ibn ʿAbbas. (p-28) Mujahid said: If a man spent all his wealth in what is right, he would not be a squanderer; and if he spent a mudd in what is not right, he would be a squanderer. Al-Zajjaj said: Tabdhir is spending in other than obedience to Allah. The Jahiliyyah used to slaughter camels and squander wealth, seeking by that boasting and reputation, so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commanded spending in its proper place, in what is near to Him.

The second: that it is extravagance (israf) that destroys wealth. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. Abu ʿUbaydah said: the mubadhdhir is the musrif, the corrupter, the one who causes ruin.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the squanderers are brothers of the devils﴾, because they agree with them in what they call them to, and resemble them in disobedience to Allah. ﴿And Satan has ever been to his Lord ungrateful﴾; that is, rejecting His blessings. This implies that the extravagant one is ungrateful for blessings.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you turn away from them﴾. Regarding those referred to there are four opinions:

The first: that they are those whose mention preceded, from the relatives, the needy and the wayfarers. This is the view of most scholars. On this view, regarding the cause of this turning away there are two opinions: The first is poverty (al-i'sar), the view of the majority. The second is fear that they would spend that in disobedience to Allah, the view of Ibn Zayd. On this view, regarding the mercy (rahmah) there are two opinions: The first is provision (rizq), the view of most scholars. The second is that it is righteousness and repentance; this is according to the view of Ibn Zayd.

The second: that they are the polytheists. The meaning then is: and if you turn away from them because of their denial, this was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr. On this view the mercy may bear two meanings: The first: awaiting victory over them. The second: guidance for them.

The third: that they were some people of Muzaynah who came asking the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for mounts, and he said: ﴿I do not find that on which I can carry you﴾, so they wept, and this verse was revealed; this was said by ʿAta' al-Khurasani. (p-29)

The fourth: that it was revealed concerning Khabbab, Bilal, ʿAmmar, Mahja', and their like among the poor, who used to ask the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and he would not find anything to give them, so he would turn away from them and be silent; this was said by Muqatil. On this view, and on the one before it, the mercy means provision (rizq).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿then speak to them a gentle word﴾. Abu ʿUbaydah said: soft and gentle, and it is from ease (yusr). The exegetes have three opinions regarding it:

The first: that it is a good promise, said by Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and Mujahid.

The second: that it is a beautiful word, such as saying: "May Allah provide for us and for you," said by Ibn Zayd, and this is in accordance with what preceded in his statement.

The third: that it is accommodating them with the tongue, according to the view of those who say they are the polytheists, said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi, and on this view the verse may admit abrogation (naskh).

The second is the obligatory maintenance (nafaqah) due to them at the time of need. The third is a bequest (wasiyyah) to them at the time of death.

It has also been said: the right of the needy is from charity, and the wayfarer's is from hospitality (al-diyafah).

The first: that it is spending wealth in what is not right. This was said by Ibn Masʿud and Ibn ʿAbbas. Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verses 29–31:

Allah's words: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck﴾. The occasion of its revelation: "A boy came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: Indeed my mother asks you for such and such. He said: 'We have nothing today.' He said: 'Then she says to you: Clothe me with your shirt.' So he (ﷺ) took off his shirt, gave it to him, and sat in the house bare-bodied, and this verse was revealed." This was narrated by Ibn Mas'ud. Jabir ibn Abd Allah narrated something similar, but added: Bilal called to prayer, and they waited for him but he did not come out, which troubled the hearts of the Companions. Some of them entered upon him and saw him naked, and then this verse was revealed.

The meaning: Do not hold your hand back from giving to the point of complete withholding, as if it were chained to your neck; ﴿and do not extend it with complete extension﴾ in giving and spending, ﴿lest you sit down reproached﴾, blaming yourself and being blamed by people, ﴿and destitute (mahsur)﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: the gift exhausts you and cuts you off, just as travel exhausts the camel so that it remains stranded and cut off. Al-Zajjaj said: the mahsur is one who has reached the utmost limit of fatigue and exhaustion; so the meaning is: you sit down having pushed yourself and your circumstances to the point where you become like one who is exhausted.

Qadi Abu Ya'la said: This address was not intended for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because he did not store anything for the next day, and he would go hungry until he tied a stone to his belly. Many of the eminent Companions would spend everything they possessed, and Allah did not forbid them, because of the soundness of their certainty. He only forbade the one who was feared to regret what had left his hand. As for one who trusts in the promise of Allah the Exalted, he is not intended by the verse.

Allah's words: ﴿Indeed your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾; that is, He widens for whom He wills and narrows. ﴿Indeed He is ever, of His servants, Acquainted and Seeing﴾, in that He apportions their provisions according to what He knows of their welfare.

Allah's words: ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾. We have explained it in (al-An'am: 151).

Allah's words: ﴿Indeed their killing has been a great sin (khit'an kabira)﴾. Nafi', Abu Amr, Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read: "khit'an" with a kasra on the kha, the ta sakin, hamzated and short. Ibn Kathir and Ata read: "khita'an" with a kasra on the kha, extended and hamzated. Ibn Amir read: "khata'an" with a fatha on the kha and ta, hamzated, without extension. Abu Razin read likewise, except that he extended it. Al-Hasan and Qatadah read: "khat'an" with a fatha on the kha, a sukun on the ta, hamzated and short. Al-Zuhri and Humayd ibn Qays read: "khita" with a kasra on the kha and tanwin on the ta, without hamza or extension. Al-Farra' said: al-khat' means sin, and it may carry the meaning of "khata'" (error), as they said: "qitb and qatab, hidhr and hadhar, najs and najas"; and al-khit', al-khita' and al-khata' (extended) are dialectal forms. Abu Ubaydah said: "khuttia" and "akhta'a" are two dialects. Abu Ali said: The reading of Ibn Kathir "khatta'" may be a verbal noun of "khata'a," even though "khata'a" is not attested, but something indicating it has come; Abu Ubaydah recited:

"Al-khat' and al-khit' and al-khatta'."

Al-Akhfash said: "khati'a yakhta'u" means "he sinned," not "he erred"; because "akhta'a" is used of what one did not do deliberately, you say of what you did deliberately: "khuttia," and of what you did not intend: "akhta'tu." Ibn al-Anbari said: al-khit' is sin; it is said: "qad khati'a yakhta'u" when one has sinned, and "akhta'a yukhti'u" when one has departed from what is right. We have explained this in (Yusuf: 91), at His words: ﴿And indeed we were among the sinners﴾.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 32–33:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not approach fornication﴾. Abu Razin, Abu al-Jawza' and al-Hasan recited it with a long vowel: al-Zina' (az-zinā'). Abu 'Ubayda said: "Al-Zina'" is also pronounced with a long vowel in the speech of the people of Najd. Al-Farazdaq said:

Abā Ḥāḍir, whoever commits fornication (yazni) will be known by his fornication, and whoever drinks the khurtum (strong wine) will in the morning be intoxicated.

And he also said:

You dyed your deed with fornication (al-zina'), and you were not one who would dye the heroes [with blood] on the day of the encounter.

And another said:

[Our saying was an obligation] just as fornication (al-zina') was an obligation for stoning.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden﴾. We have mentioned it in (al-An'am: 151).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We have given﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The better (al-ajwad) is to assimilate the dal into the jim (idgham), and clear pronunciation (al-izhar) is also good and sufficient, except that the jim comes from the middle of the tongue and the dal from the tip of the tongue, and assimilation is permissible because the letters of the middle of the tongue are close to the letters of the tip of the tongue. Its walī (guardian) is the one between whom and the victim there is a kinship that entitles him to demand his blood. If he has no walī, then the sultan is his walī.

Regarding "the sultan," the exegetes have two opinions:

One: that it is the proof (al-hujja). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: that it is the ruler (al-wali), and the meaning is: We have given to his guardian authority (sultan) who will support him and grant him justice regarding his right. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿but let him not commit excess in killing﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and 'Asim recited it: (fa-lā yusrif) with the yā' (ya). Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited it with the tā' (ta).

Regarding the one referred to in the verse there are two opinions:

(p-33) One: that it is the guardian of the one killed. Regarding the meaning of his excess there are five opinions: First: that he kills someone other than the killer, said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan. Second: that he kills two for one, said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Third: that he kills someone more noble than the one who was killed, said by Ibn Zayd. Fourth: that he mutilates, said by Qatada. Fifth: that he himself takes the killing of the killer instead of the sultan, mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

The second: that the reference is to the first killer, and the meaning is: let the killer not commit excess in killing by transgressing and wronging, said by Mujahid.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he was supported﴾; that is, he was helped (mu'an 'alayhi).

Regarding the pronoun of reference (ha' al-kinaya) there are four opinions:

First: that it refers to the guardian; the meaning is: indeed he was supported by being empowered with retaliation (al-qawad), said by Qatada and the majority.

The second: that it refers to the one killed; the meaning is: he was supported by the killing of his killer, said by Mujahid.

The third: that it refers to the blood; the meaning is: the blood of the one killed was supported; that is, it was sought (matlub) by him.

The fourth: that it refers to the killing; al-Farra' mentioned both opinions.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 34–36:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan﴾. We have explained this in (al-An'am: 152).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And fulfill the covenant﴾. It is general, concerning what is between the servant and his Lord, and what is between him and the people. Al-Zajjaj said: Everything that Allah has commanded and forbidden is part of the covenant.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, it is ever questioned﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: That is, it will be questioned about it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And give full measure when you measure﴾; that is, complete it and do not diminish from it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And weigh with an even balance﴾. In it there are five dialects (lughat). The first: (qusTas) with a dammah on the qaf and two sins (s), and this is the reading of Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim here and in (ash-Shu'ara: 182). The second is similar, except that the qaf is kasrah, and this is the reading of Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim. Al-Farra' said: They are two dialects. The third: (qusTaS) with two sads. The fourth: (qusTas) with a sad before the ta' and a sin after it, and these two are reported from Hamzah. The fifth: (qistan) with an nun. I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi, from Ibn Duraid, who said: al-qistas is the balance, a Roman word that has been Arabized, and it is said: qistas and qustas.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is better﴾; that is, that fulfilling is better with Allah and closer to Him, ﴿and better in outcome﴾; that is, better in its end in terms of recompense.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge﴾. Al-Farra' said: The origin of taqf is from qiyafah, which is tracking a trail. There are two dialects: qafa yaqfu and qaafa yaquf. Most readers take it from (qafawtu), so the fa' is moved to the waw and the qaf is jazm, as you say: la tad'u. Mu'adh al-Qari' read: (la taquf), like taqul. The Arabs say: quftu athrahu and qafawtu, and similar to it: 'aatha wa'than, and qa'a al-jamalu an-naqata and qa'ahā, when he rode her. Al-Zajjaj said: Whoever reads with the fa' sukun and the qaf dammah, from qaafa yaquf, it is as if it is inverted from qafa yaqfu, and the meaning is one. You say: qafawtu ash-shay'a aqfuhu qafwan, if you follow its trail. Ibn Qutaybah said: ﴿wa la taqf﴾; that is, do not follow it with assumptions and conjecture, and it is derived from qafa', as if you are following matters; that is, you are at their backs and ends, pursuing them, and the qa'if is the one who knows traces and follows them, so it is as if it is inverted from al-qafi.

For the exegetes there are four opinions regarding its meaning:

The first: Do not accuse anyone of what you have no knowledge of. Al-'Awfi related it from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: Do not say: "I saw," when you did not see, nor "I heard," when you did not hear. 'Uthman ibn 'Ata related it from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatadah said likewise.

The third: Do not associate anything with Allah. 'Ata also related it from Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: Do not bear false witness. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said this.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the hearing and the sight and the heart — all of those﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: He said "kull," then said "kana," because kull is in the singular form, and he said "ula'ika" for non-humans, because every plural I point to among humans and others, including the lifeless, you point to with the word "ula'ika." Jarir said:

Blame the dwellings after the abode of al-Liwa, and life after those days.

The exegetes said: The reference is to the mentioned limbs; the servant will be asked on the Day of Resurrection about how he used them. In this is a warning against looking at what is not lawful, listening to what is forbidden, and resolving upon what is not permissible.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 37–39:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly﴾. Al-Dahhak and Ibn Yu'mur recited "maraḥan" (مَرِحًا) with a kasra on the ra'. Al-Akhfash said: "The kasra is better, because "mari<u>h</u>an" is the active participle (ism al-fa'il)." Al-Zajjaj said: "Both are equal in soundness, except that the verbal noun (masdar) is more emphatic in usage. You say: 'Zayd came running' (jā'a Zaydun rakḍan), and 'Zayd came running' (jā'a Zaydun rākiḍan); so 'rakḍan' is more emphatic in usage, because it indicates the emphasis of the verb." The meaning of the verse is: Do not walk upon the earth arrogant and boastful. Al-Maraḥ is insolence and wantonness. Ibn Faris said: al-maraḥ is intense joy.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you will never tear through the earth﴾. In it there are two opinions:

One: you will never cross it to its end. The second: you will never pierce it and bore through it. Ibn 'Abbas said: "You will never tear through the earth with your pride, and you will never reach the mountains in height with your greatness." Ibn Qutayba said: "The meaning is: it is not fitting for the powerless to boast and act haughty."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿All of that was its evil (sayyi'uhu) is hateful to your Lord﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr recited "sayyi'atun" (سَيِّئَةٌ) with tanwin and without an annexed noun, meaning: "it was a wrongdoing (khati'ah)." According to this reading, His saying "kullu dhalika" (all of that) refers only to what was forbidden among what was mentioned. 'Asim, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and al-Kisa'i recited "sayyi'uhu" (سَيِّئُهُ) annexed and masculine, so the word "kull" (all) refers to all that was mentioned previously. Abu 'Amr did not approve of this reading. Al-Zajjaj said: "This is an error on the part of Abu 'Amr, because in these narrations there is both evil and good. Indeed, in them is the command to be dutiful to the parents, to give to the near kin, to fulfil the covenant, and the like. Therefore this reading is better than the reading of the one who put the sayyi'ah in the accusative." Likewise Abu 'Ubayda said: "I reflected on the verses from His saying, ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾, and I found in them good matters." Abu 'Ali said: "Whoever recites 'sayyi'atan' regards the speech as ending at His saying, ﴿and better in interpretation﴾, and that His saying, ﴿And do not pursue﴾ has no goodness in it."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This is of what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom﴾ refers to what preceded of obligations and recommended practices, ﴿of wisdom﴾; that is, of firm matters and good manners that gather every good. The meaning of "al-madhur" (the rejected) has already been explained (al-A'raf: 18).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 40:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Has your Lord then chosen you for sons⁠—﴾ Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning the polytheists of the Arabs who said: "The angels are the daughters of the Most Merciful." Abu Ubayda said: The meaning of ﴿afa-asfakum﴾ ("has He then chosen you") is: He singled you out (ikhtassakum). Al-Mufaddal said: He purified you for Himself (akhlasakum). Al-Zajjaj said: He chose for you the pure essence (safwa) of a thing. This is a rebuke to the disbelievers, and the meaning is: He chose sons for you, to the exclusion of Himself, and made daughters shared between you and Him, so He singled you out with the superior and assigned to Himself the inferior.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 41:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We have certainly diversified⦆ (wa-laqad sarrafna). The meaning of al-tasrif (diversification) here is al-tabyin (clarification), because one only varies speech in order to make it clear. Ibn Qutayba said: "sarrafna" means "wajjahna" (We directed), and it is from your saying: "saraftu ilayka kadha," i.e., "I turned such-and-such toward you," and it is doubled (in form) for intensification, just as you say: "fatahtu al-abwab" (I opened the doors).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿that they may take heed⦆ (li-yadhdhakkaru). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read (li-yadhdhakkaru) with the doubled dal. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read (li-dhakkaru) without doubling, and they read likewise in (al-Furqan: 50). Al-tadhakkur means al-it'az (being admonished) and al-tadabbur (reflection). ﴿But it only increases them⦆ (wa-ma yaziduhum), i.e., Our diversification and Our reminding, ﴿in nothing but aversion⦆ (illa nufura). Ibn 'Abbas said: they flee from the truth and follow falsehood.

Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary on Surah 17, verses 42–44 (Zad al-Masir)

Ibn al-Jawzi on His words, ﴿Say: "Had there been with Him gods, as they claim, they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne."﴾ Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read ﴿taqulun﴾ with a ta' (second person). Ibn Kathir and Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read ﴿yaqulun﴾ with a ya' (third person).

His words, ﴿they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾ have two interpretations:

First: they would have sought a way to oppose Him and to remove His dominion. This is the view of al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Second: they would have sought a way to His pleasure, because they are beneath Him. This is the view of Qatada.

His words, ﴿above what they say﴾ are read by Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr, and Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, with ya' (﴿yaqulun﴾). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with ta' (﴿taqulun﴾). [p-39]

His words, ﴿The seven heavens glorify Him﴾ are read by Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, with ta' (﴿tusabbihu﴾). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read it with ya' (﴿yusabbihu﴾). Al-Farra' said: The ya' is preferred here because the number is small, and when the number of feminine or masculine nouns is small, the ya' is better than the ta'. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said of a small feminine group: ﴿And women said﴾ [Yusuf 30], and of a masculine group: ﴿Then when the sacred months have passed﴾ [al-Tawbah 5]. The scholars said: The meaning of this glorification is that it indicates that He is the Creator, the All-Powerful.

His words, ﴿There is not a thing but glorifies Him with His praise﴾: ( إنْ ) here has the meaning of ( ما ). Is this to be taken in its absolute sense or not? There are two views:

First: it is to be taken in its absolute sense, so everything glorifies Him, even clothing, food, and the creaking of a door. This is the view of Ibrahim al-Nakha'i.

Second: it is general, but a specific sense is intended. Within this view there are three opinions:

One: everything that has a soul. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatada, and al-Dahhak.

Two: every living being, and every growing thing of trees or plants. 'Ikrima said: The tree glorifies, but the pillar does not glorify. Al-Hasan sat down to a meal, and when the table was brought, he was asked: "Does this table glorify?" He said: "It once did glorify."

Three: everything that has not been changed from its state. When it changes, its glorification ceases. Khalid ibn Ma'dan narrated from al-Miqdam ibn Ma'di Karib, who said: "Indeed the dust glorifies as long as it is not moistened; when it becomes moist, it stops glorifying. Indeed the leaf glorifies as long as it is on the tree; when it falls, it stops glorifying. Indeed the garment glorifies as long as it is new; when it becomes soiled, it stops glorifying."

As for the glorification of the rational living being, it is well known. As for the glorification of non-rational living beings, it is possible that it is by their voice, and it is possible that it is by their indication of their Maker.

Regarding the glorification of inanimate things, there are three opinions:
