Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary on Surah 17, verses 42–44 (Zad al-Masir)

Ibn al-Jawzi on His words, ﴿Say: "Had there been with Him gods, as they claim, they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne."﴾ Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read ﴿taqulun﴾ with a ta' (second person). Ibn Kathir and Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read ﴿yaqulun﴾ with a ya' (third person).

His words, ﴿they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾ have two interpretations:

First: they would have sought a way to oppose Him and to remove His dominion. This is the view of al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Second: they would have sought a way to His pleasure, because they are beneath Him. This is the view of Qatada.

His words, ﴿above what they say﴾ are read by Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr, and Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, with ya' (﴿yaqulun﴾). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read it with ta' (﴿taqulun﴾). [p-39]

His words, ﴿The seven heavens glorify Him﴾ are read by Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, with ta' (﴿tusabbihu﴾). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read it with ya' (﴿yusabbihu﴾). Al-Farra' said: The ya' is preferred here because the number is small, and when the number of feminine or masculine nouns is small, the ya' is better than the ta'. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said of a small feminine group: ﴿And women said﴾ [Yusuf 30], and of a masculine group: ﴿Then when the sacred months have passed﴾ [al-Tawbah 5]. The scholars said: The meaning of this glorification is that it indicates that He is the Creator, the All-Powerful.

His words, ﴿There is not a thing but glorifies Him with His praise﴾: ( إنْ ) here has the meaning of ( ما ). Is this to be taken in its absolute sense or not? There are two views:

First: it is to be taken in its absolute sense, so everything glorifies Him, even clothing, food, and the creaking of a door. This is the view of Ibrahim al-Nakha'i.

Second: it is general, but a specific sense is intended. Within this view there are three opinions:

One: everything that has a soul. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatada, and al-Dahhak.

Two: every living being, and every growing thing of trees or plants. 'Ikrima said: The tree glorifies, but the pillar does not glorify. Al-Hasan sat down to a meal, and when the table was brought, he was asked: "Does this table glorify?" He said: "It once did glorify."

Three: everything that has not been changed from its state. When it changes, its glorification ceases. Khalid ibn Ma'dan narrated from al-Miqdam ibn Ma'di Karib, who said: "Indeed the dust glorifies as long as it is not moistened; when it becomes moist, it stops glorifying. Indeed the leaf glorifies as long as it is on the tree; when it falls, it stops glorifying. Indeed the garment glorifies as long as it is new; when it becomes soiled, it stops glorifying."

"A veil that is hidden" (ḥijāban mastūran). There are three opinions on this:

The first: the veil is the coverings (akinnah) over their hearts. This is the view of Qatadah.

The second: it is a veil that conceals it, so that you do not see it. It was also said that this was revealed concerning a people who used to harm the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when he recited the Qur'an. Al-Kalbi said: they were Abu Sufyan, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abu Jahl, and Umm Jamil the wife of Abu Lahab. So Allah veiled His Messenger from their sight during the recitation of the Qur'an, so they would come to him and pass by him, yet not see him.

The third: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, prevented them from harming him. This is related by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding the meaning of "hidden" (mastūran), there are two views:

One: it carries the sense of "concealing" (sātir). Al-Zajjaj said: this is the view of the lexicographers. Al-Akhfash said: the active participle may appear in the form of the passive, as you say: "You are ill-omened (mashʾūm) for us" and "auspicious (maymūn) for us," when the intended forms are shā'im and yāmin, because it derives from "their ill omen (sha'mihim) and their blessing (yumnihim)."

Two: the meaning is "a veil hidden from you, so that you do not see it." This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. Ibn al-Anbari said: if it is said that the veil is the sealing (ṭab') upon their hearts, then it is "hidden" from the sight, and so "mastūran" remains on its own form.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it﴾. We have explained this in (al-An'am: 25).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an﴾ means: when you say, "There is no god but Allah," while you are reciting the Qur'an, ﴿they turn away on their backs﴾. Abu Ubaydah said: that is, on their heels. "Nufuran" is the plural of nafir, like qa'id and qu'ud, and jalis and julus. Al-Zajjaj said: it admits two interpretations: one, that it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), so the meaning is "they turned away in aversion (nafiran nufuran)." The second: that "nufuran" is the plural of nafir.

Regarding those referred to, there are two views: one, that they are the devils, related from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second, that they are the polytheists, which is the view of Ibn Zayd.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We know best what they listen to when they listen to you﴾. The exegetes said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded ʿAli, peace be upon him, to prepare a meal and invite to it the nobles of Quraysh from among the polytheists. He did so, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered upon them and recited the Qur'an to them, and invited them to monotheism. They were listening and saying among themselves: 'He is a sorcerer, he is bewitched.' So this verse was revealed: ﴿We know best what they listen to when they listen to you﴾"; that is, they listen to it, and the ba' is extra. ﴿When they listen to you, and when they are in private conference﴾. Abu Ubaydah said: "najwa" is a verbal noun from "najaytu" and also a noun from it, so he described the people by it, and the Arabs do this, as in their saying: "It is only a punishment, and you are a grief," so it came in the place of "mutanajin" (those conferring privately). Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "when they are people of private conference," and they used to listen to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and say among themselves: "He is a sorcerer, he is bewitched," and what resembles that of speech.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When the wrongdoers say﴾, meaning those polytheists, ﴿You follow only a man bewitched﴾; that is, "What you follow." And regarding it there are three opinions:

One: that he is the one who was bewitched so that his mind was taken away. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: deceived and deluded. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: he has a "sihr," that is, a windpipe (ri'ah), and every animal, bird, or human that eats is "maswur" and "musahhar," because it has a "sihr." Labid said:

"So if you ask us what our state is, we are sparrows among this musahhar (fed) creature."

And Imru' al-Qays said:

"We see ourselves watching for an unseen matter, and we are fed (nuhsar) with food and drink."

That is: we are nourished, because the people of heaven do not eat, so he wanted to be a king. According to this, the meaning is: "You follow only a man who has a windpipe, whom Allah created like you, and is not a king." This is the view of Abu Ubaydah.

Ibn Qutaybah said: the correct view is that of Mujahid [that is, deceived], because sorcery is trickery and deception, and the meaning of Labid's words "al-musahhar" is "the one given reasons (mu'allal)," and the meaning of Imru' al-Qays's "nuhsar" is "nu'allal" (we are given reasons), as if we are deceived. People say: "You have bewitched me with your words," that is, "You have deceived me." This is supported by His saying: ﴿See how they strike for you the parables﴾, because if they had meant a man with a windpipe, there would be no parable in that which they struck. But when they meant "a deceived man," as if by deception he had been bewitched, it became a parable they struck. It is as if they went to the view that some people taught him and deceived him. The exegetes said: the meaning of ﴿they struck for you the parables﴾ is: they explained to you the likenesses, until they likened you to the sorcerer, the poet, and the madman. ﴿So they have gone astray﴾ from the truth, ﴿and they cannot find a way﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions:

One: they do not find a way to correct what they blame you for.

The second: they cannot find a way to guidance, because We have sealed their hearts.

The third: they do not come to the path of truth because it is heavy upon them. A similar expression is their saying: "I cannot look at so-and-so," meaning: "I hate him, so looking at him is burdensome to me." This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When we are bones...﴾ Ibn Kathir recited: "a-idha" with a hamzah, then he comes with a silent ya' without elongation; "ayyanna" is similar to it, and so throughout the Qur'an. Qalun related likewise from Nafi', except that Nafi' did not make the second word an interrogative in "ayyana"; he made the second a statement throughout the Qur'an. This is also the school of al-Kisa'i, except that he made the first hamzah a double hamzah. ʿAsim and Hamzah recited with two hamzahs in both words. Ibn ʿAmir recited "idha kunna" without interrogation, with a single hamzah, and "a-inna" with two hamzahs, elongating between them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and rufatan﴾. Regarding it there are two opinions:

One: it is dust, and it has no singular, so it is like "daqaq" and "hutam" (crumbs and debris). This was said by al-Farra', and it is the view of Mujahid.

The second: it is the bones that have not been broken, and the rufat is the debris. This was said by Abu Ubaydah. Al-Zajjaj said: rufat is dust. And rufat is everything that has been smashed and broken. And ﴿a new creation﴾ means "renewed."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿or a creation of what is greater in your breasts﴾. Regarding it there are three opinions:

One: it is death. This was said by Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and most of the scholars.

The second: it is the heaven, the earth, and the mountains. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: [it is] what is greatest in your breasts of all that you consider great of Allah's creation. This was said by Qatadah.

If it is asked: how is it said to them, ﴿Be stones or iron﴾, when they are not able to do that? There are two answers:

One: if you are able to change your states, then be stones or harder than them, for We will still cause you to die and execute Our judgments upon you. A similar statement is your saying to a man: "Ascend to the heaven, for I will overtake you."

The second: imagine yourselves as stones or harder than them, for We will surely annihilate you. Al-Ahwas said:

"If you are one who abstains from play and youth, then be a stone, a boulder of dry hard rock."

Its meaning: "Imagine yourself a stone." These people acknowledged that Allah is their Creator but denied the resurrection, so they were informed that He who originated their creation is the One who will give them life.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So they will shake their heads toward you﴾. Qatadah said: they will move them in denial and mockery. Al-Farra' said: it is said: "anghada ra'sahu" when he moves it upward and downward. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is: they move them, as one despairing of something or deeming it far-fetched moves his head; it is said: "naghadat sinnuhu" when his tooth moves.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they say, "When is it?"﴾ meaning: the resurrection. ﴿Say, "It may be that it is near."﴾ That is: it is near. Then explain when it will be, so He said: ﴿On the Day He calls you﴾, meaning: from the graves, by the call that will hear you, which is the last blast, ﴿and you will respond﴾; that is, you will answer. Muqatil said: Israfil will stand on the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis, calling the people of the graves with a horn, and say: "O decayed bones, O torn flesh, O scattered hair, O severed veins, come out to the place of judgment to be recompensed for your deeds." They will hear the voice and hasten toward it.

Regarding the meaning of "bi-hamdihi" there are four opinions:

One: by His command. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jurayj, and Ibn Zayd.

The second: they will come out of the graves saying, "Glory be to You and praise be to You." This was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The third: that the meaning of "bi-hamdihi" is with knowledge of Him and obedience to Him. This was said by Qatadah. Al-Zajjaj said: you will respond acknowledging that He is your Creator.

The fourth: you will respond with the praise of Allah, not with the praise of yourselves. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you will think that you remained not but a little﴾. Regarding this supposition there are two opinions:

One: it carries the meaning of certainty.

The second: it is on its original sense. Where do they suppose they remained only a little? Regarding this there are three opinions: One: between the two blasts, and its duration is forty years, during which the punishment is cut off from them, so they consider their stay in the time of rest to be little. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: in the world, because of their knowledge of the length of the stay in the Hereafter. This was said by al-Hasan. The third: in the graves. This was said by Muqatil. According to this, the stay in the graves appears short to them because they went out to something far greater in punishment than the punishment of the graves. Some exegetes went to the view that this verse is addressed to the believers, because they respond to the caller while praising Allah for His kindness to them, and they consider the duration of the stay in the graves to be little, because they were not punished.

One: it is dust, and it has no singular, so it is like "daqaq" and "hutam" (crumbs and debris). This was said by al-Farra', and it is the view of Mujahid.

The second: it is the bones that have not been broken, and the rufat is the debris. This was said by Abu Ubaydah. Al-Zajjaj said: rufat is dust. And rufat is everything that has been smashed and broken. And ﴿a new creation﴾ means "renewed."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿or a creation of what is greater in your breasts﴾. Regarding it there are three opinions:

One: it is death. This was said by Ibn ʿUmar, Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and most of the scholars.

The second: it is the heaven, the earth, and the mountains. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: [it is] what is greatest in your breasts of all that you consider great of Allah's creation. This was said by Qatadah.

If it is asked: how is it said to them, ﴿Be stones or iron﴾, when they are not able to do that? There are two answers:

One: if you are able to change your states, then be stones or harder than them, for We will still cause you to die and execute Our judgments upon you. A similar statement is your saying to a man: "Ascend to the heaven, for I will overtake you."

The second: imagine yourselves as stones or harder than them, for We will surely annihilate you. Al-Ahwas said:

"If you are one who abstains from play and youth, then be a stone, a boulder of dry hard rock."

Its meaning: "Imagine yourself a stone." These people acknowledged that Allah is their Creator but denied the resurrection, so they were informed that He who originated their creation is the One who will give them life.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So they will shake their heads toward you﴾. Qatadah said: they will move them in denial and mockery. Al-Farra' said: it is said: "anghada ra'sahu" when he moves it upward and downward. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is: they move them, as one despairing of something or deeming it far-fetched moves his head; it is said: "naghadat sinnuhu" when his tooth moves.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they say, "When is it?"﴾ meaning: the resurrection. ﴿Say, "It may be that it is near."﴾ That is: it is near. Then explain when it will be, so He said: ﴿On the Day He calls you﴾, meaning: from the graves, by the call that will hear you, which is the last blast, ﴿and you will respond﴾; that is, you will answer. Muqatil said: Israfil will stand on the rock of Bayt al-Maqdis, calling the people of the graves with a horn, and say: "O decayed bones, O torn flesh, O scattered hair, O severed veins, come out to the place of judgment to be recompensed for your deeds." They will hear the voice and hasten toward it.

Regarding the meaning of "bi-hamdihi" there are four opinions:

One: by His command. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Jurayj, and Ibn Zayd.

The second: they will come out of the graves saying, "Glory be to You and praise be to You." This was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The third: that the meaning of "bi-hamdihi" is with knowledge of Him and obedience to Him. This was said by Qatadah. Al-Zajjaj said: you will respond acknowledging that He is your Creator.

The fourth: you will respond with the praise of Allah, not with the praise of yourselves. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you will think that you remained not but a little﴾. Regarding this supposition there are two opinions:

One: it carries the meaning of certainty.

The second: it is on its original sense. Where do they suppose they remained only a little? Regarding this there are three opinions: One: between the two blasts, and its duration is forty years, during which the punishment is cut off from them, so they consider their stay in the time of rest to be little. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: in the world, because of their knowledge of the length of the stay in the Hereafter. This was said by al-Hasan. The third: in the graves. This was said by Muqatil. According to this, the stay in the graves appears short to them because they went out to something far greater in punishment than the punishment of the graves. Some exegetes went to the view that this verse is addressed to the believers, because they respond to the caller while praising Allah for His kindness to them, and they consider the duration of the stay in the graves to be little, because they were not punished.

"A veil that is hidden" (ḥijāban mastūran). There are three opinions on this:

The first: the veil is the coverings (akinnah) over their hearts. This is the view of Qatadah.

The second: it is a veil that conceals it, so that you do not see it. It was also said that this was revealed concerning a people who used to harm the Messenger of Allah ﷺ when he recited the Qur'an. Al-Kalbi said: they were Abu Sufyan, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Abu Jahl, and Umm Jamil the wife of Abu Lahab. So Allah veiled His Messenger from their sight during the recitation of the Qur'an, so they would come to him and pass by him, yet not see him.

The third: Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, prevented them from harming him. This is related by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding the meaning of "hidden" (mastūran), there are two views:

One: it carries the sense of "concealing" (sātir). Al-Zajjaj said: this is the view of the lexicographers. Al-Akhfash said: the active participle may appear in the form of the passive, as you say: "You are ill-omened (mashʾūm) for us" and "auspicious (maymūn) for us," when the intended forms are shā'im and yāmin, because it derives from "their ill omen (sha'mihim) and their blessing (yumnihim)."

Two: the meaning is "a veil hidden from you, so that you do not see it." This was mentioned by al-Mawardi. Ibn al-Anbari said: if it is said that the veil is the sealing (ṭab') upon their hearts, then it is "hidden" from the sight, and so "mastūran" remains on its own form.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it﴾. We have explained this in (al-An'am: 25).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an﴾ means: when you say, "There is no god but Allah," while you are reciting the Qur'an, ﴿they turn away on their backs﴾. Abu Ubaydah said: that is, on their heels. "Nufuran" is the plural of nafir, like qa'id and qu'ud, and jalis and julus. Al-Zajjaj said: it admits two interpretations: one, that it is a verbal noun (maṣdar), so the meaning is "they turned away in aversion (nafiran nufuran)." The second: that "nufuran" is the plural of nafir.

Regarding those referred to, there are two views: one, that they are the devils, related from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second, that they are the polytheists, which is the view of Ibn Zayd.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿We know best what they listen to when they listen to you﴾. The exegetes said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded ʿAli, peace be upon him, to prepare a meal and invite to it the nobles of Quraysh from among the polytheists. He did so, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered upon them and recited the Qur'an to them, and invited them to monotheism. They were listening and saying among themselves: 'He is a sorcerer, he is bewitched.' So this verse was revealed: ﴿We know best what they listen to when they listen to you﴾"; that is, they listen to it, and the ba' is extra. ﴿When they listen to you, and when they are in private conference﴾. Abu Ubaydah said: "najwa" is a verbal noun from "najaytu" and also a noun from it, so he described the people by it, and the Arabs do this, as in their saying: "It is only a punishment, and you are a grief," so it came in the place of "mutanajin" (those conferring privately). Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "when they are people of private conference," and they used to listen to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and say among themselves: "He is a sorcerer, he is bewitched," and what resembles that of speech.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When the wrongdoers say﴾, meaning those polytheists, ﴿You follow only a man bewitched﴾; that is, "What you follow." And regarding it there are three opinions:

One: that he is the one who was bewitched so that his mind was taken away. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: deceived and deluded. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: he has a "sihr," that is, a windpipe (ri'ah), and every animal, bird, or human that eats is "maswur" and "musahhar," because it has a "sihr." Labid said:

"So if you ask us what our state is, we are sparrows among this musahhar (fed) creature."

And Imru' al-Qays said:

"We see ourselves watching for an unseen matter, and we are fed (nuhsar) with food and drink."

That is: we are nourished, because the people of heaven do not eat, so he wanted to be a king. According to this, the meaning is: "You follow only a man who has a windpipe, whom Allah created like you, and is not a king." This is the view of Abu Ubaydah.

Ibn Qutaybah said: the correct view is that of Mujahid [that is, deceived], because sorcery is trickery and deception, and the meaning of Labid's words "al-musahhar" is "the one given reasons (mu'allal)," and the meaning of Imru' al-Qays's "nuhsar" is "nu'allal" (we are given reasons), as if we are deceived. People say: "You have bewitched me with your words," that is, "You have deceived me." This is supported by His saying: ﴿See how they strike for you the parables﴾, because if they had meant a man with a windpipe, there would be no parable in that which they struck. But when they meant "a deceived man," as if by deception he had been bewitched, it became a parable they struck. It is as if they went to the view that some people taught him and deceived him. The exegetes said: the meaning of ﴿they struck for you the parables﴾ is: they explained to you the likenesses, until they likened you to the sorcerer, the poet, and the madman. ﴿So they have gone astray﴾ from the truth, ﴿and they cannot find a way﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions:

One: they do not find a way to correct what they blame you for.

The second: they cannot find a way to guidance, because We have sealed their hearts.

The third: they do not come to the path of truth because it is heavy upon them. A similar expression is their saying: "I cannot look at so-and-so," meaning: "I hate him, so looking at him is burdensome to me." This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When we are bones...﴾ Ibn Kathir recited: "a-idha" with a hamzah, then he comes with a silent ya' without elongation; "ayyanna" is similar to it, and so throughout the Qur'an. Qalun related likewise from Nafi', except that Nafi' did not make the second word an interrogative in "ayyana"; he made the second a statement throughout the Qur'an. This is also the school of al-Kisa'i, except that he made the first hamzah a double hamzah. ʿAsim and Hamzah recited with two hamzahs in both words. Ibn ʿAmir recited "idha kunna" without interrogation, with a single hamzah, and "a-inna" with two hamzahs, elongating between them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 53:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And tell My servants to say that which is best﴾. Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are two accounts:

One: The polytheists used to harm the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in Makkah, with words and deeds, so they complained of that to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and this verse was revealed. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn Abbas.

The second: A man from among the disbelievers insulted Umar ibn al-Khattab, so Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) intended to strike him, and this verse was revealed. This was said by Muqatil. The meaning is: "And tell My servants, the believers, to say the word that is best." They differed about to whom this word is to be said, on two views:

One: They are the polytheists. Al-Hasan said: you say to him, "May Allah guide you." The account of the occasion of revelation mentioned above supports this view. Some scholars held that they were commanded with this verse to speak courteously to the polytheists before being commanded to fight them, and then this verse was abrogated by the verse of the sword.

The second: They are the Muslims. This was said by Ibn Jarir. The meaning is: "And tell My servants that some of them should say to others the word that is best, in conversation and address." Mubarak narrated from al-Hasan, who said: "That which is best" means that he says to him the like of what he said, but rather he says to him: "May Allah have mercy on you" and "May Allah forgive you." Al-Akhfash said: His saying "yaqulu" (they say) is like His saying "yuqimu" (they establish) in "yuqimu as-salah" (establish the prayer), and we have explained that in Surah Ibrahim (14:31).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Satan incites [discord] among them﴾; that is, he corrupts what is between them. And "clear enemy" means one whose enmity is evident.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 54:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Your Lord knows you best.﴾ Concerning whom this was addressed, there are two opinions:

The first: they are the believers. Then, regarding the meaning of the speech, there are two views. One: ﴿If He wills, He will have mercy upon you﴾ by saving you from the people of Makkah, and ﴿if He wills, He will punish you﴾ by giving them power over you. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: if He wills, He will have mercy upon you through repentance, or punish you through persisting in sins. This was said by al-Hasan. (p-48)

The second: they are the polytheists. Then, regarding the meaning of the speech, there are two views. One: if He wills, He will have mercy upon you and guide you to faith, or if He wills, He will punish you and cause you to die in disbelief. This was said by Muqatil. The second: when famine struck the polytheists, they said: ﴿Our Lord, remove the punishment from us; indeed we are believers﴾ [al-Dukhan: 12]. Allah, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Your Lord knows you best﴾ as to who believes and who does not believe. ﴿If He wills, He will have mercy upon you﴾ by lifting the famine from you, ﴿or if He wills, He will punish you﴾ by leaving it upon you. This was mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. Ibn al-Anbari said: "aw" (or) entered here to express the breadth of both matters with Allah, may He be exalted, and that neither of them is turned away from Him. Thus it was attached to the permissive "aw" in their saying: "Al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin sat with him," meaning: "We have granted you leeway in the matter."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We did not send you as a guardian over them.﴾ Concerning this there are three views:

The first: a guarantor who will be held responsible for them. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: a guardian and a lord. This was said by al-Farra'. The third: a guarantor of their guidance and one able to correct their hearts. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. Some exegetes held that this is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 55:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord knows best who is in the heavens and the earth﴾; because He is their Creator, so He guides whom He wills and sends astray whom He wills. Likewise, He preferred some of the prophets over others, and that is from His wisdom and knowledge. He created Adam with His own hand, raised up Idris, made the descendants to be from Nuh, took Ibrahim as a close friend (khalil), spoke directly to Musa (kalim), made Isa a spirit, gave Sulayman a great kingdom, and raised Muhammad (ﷺ) above the heavens, and forgave him what was past of his sin and what was to come. It is also possible that the ones preferred are the people of the Books, because He concluded the speech with His saying: ﴿And We gave Dawud the Zabur﴾. We have already explained the meaning of "al-Zabur" in surah al-Nisa (4:163).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verses 56–57:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Call upon those whom you claim besides Him﴾. Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are two views:

One: a group of the Arabs used to worship a group of the jinn, then the jinn embraced Islam while the group of Arabs did not realize it. So this verse and the one after it were revealed. This is related from Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: the polytheists used to worship the angels, saying, "They intercede for us with God." When they were afflicted with drought for seven years, it was said to them: ﴿Call upon those whom you claim﴾. This is what Muqatil said. The meaning: Say, "Call upon those whom you claim to be gods, ﴿and they have no power to remove the harm from you, nor to change it [to another]﴾," meaning to transfer it to anyone other than you.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those whom they call upon themselves seek the means of access to their Lord﴾. Concerning those referred to by "those" (ulaika), there are three views:

One: they are the jinn who embraced Islam. The second: the angels, and the explanation of these two views has already passed. The third: they are the Messiah, 'Uzayr, the angels, the sun and the moon. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas. Concerning the meaning of "call upon" (yad'un), there are two views:

One: it means "worship"; that is, they call upon them as gods. This is the view of the majority.

The second: it means "entreat God" in seeking the means of access (wasila). On this view, his saying "call upon" (yad'un) refers back to "those" (ulaika), and his saying "they seek" (yabtaghun) is a completion of the sentence. On the first view, "call upon" (yad'un) refers back to the polytheists, and his saying "they seek" (yabtaghun) is a descriptive clause for "those," resumed as a new sentence. Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read (tad'una) with the letter ta'. Ibn al-Anbari said: On this reading, the verb is directed back to his saying: ﴿they have no power to remove the harm from you﴾. As for the one who reads (yad'una) with the letter ya', he says: the Arabs shift from address (khitab) to third person (ghayba) when there is no ambiguity. The meaning of "call upon" is: they call upon them as gods. We have already explained the meaning of ﴿the means of access (al-wasila)﴾ in (al-Ma'ida: 35).

Concerning his saying: ﴿which of them is nearest﴾, there are two views, mentioned by al-Zajjaj:

One: that "which of them" (ayyuhum) is in the nominative as the subject, and its predicate is "nearest" (aqrab). The meaning is: they seek the means of access to their Lord, looking to see which of them is nearest to Him, so that they seek access to God through him.

The second: that "which of them is nearest" is a substitute (badal) for the waw in "they seek" (yabtaghun), so the meaning is: they seek which of them is nearest, the means of access to God; that is, they draw near to Him through righteous deeds.

Allah's words: ﴿And there is no town but We will destroy it before the Day of Resurrection or punish it with a severe punishment. That is written in the Book.﴾ Here "in" (إنْ) carries the meaning of "ma" (ما), and the righteous town's destruction is by death, while the disobedient town's is by punishment. "The Book" is the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), and "inscribed" (al-mastur) means written.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 59:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We did not refrain from sending the signs⦆ There are two views regarding the occasion of its revelation:

The first: "The people of Makkah asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to turn al-Safa into gold for them and to remove the mountains from them so that they could farm. It was said to him: 'If you wish, we will give you respite with them, perhaps we will choose from among them; and if you wish, we will give them what they asked for, but if they disbelieve, they will be destroyed as those before them were destroyed.' He said: 'No, rather I will give them respite.' So this verse was revealed." Narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: We have already mentioned it from al-Zubayr regarding His saying: ﴿And if a Qur'an by which the mountains were moved⦆ [al-Ra'd: 31]. The meaning of the verse is: "What prevented Us from sending the signs they asked for was only the denial of the earlier peoples." That is, these people asked for the signs for which the earlier people deserved punishment upon denying them, so He did not send them, lest these people deny them and be destroyed as those were destroyed. The custom of Allah regarding the nations is that when they ask for signs and then deny them, He punishes them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign⦆ Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, a clear proof, meaning "one who sees by means of it." Ibn al-Anbari said: It is also permissible that it be mubsirah (causing sight), and it is suitable that the meaning be "mubsir" (seeing) in the sense of its viewers, so the act of others is attributed to it figuratively, as one says: "I will not let you see me here," where the prohibitive particle is applied to other than the one forbidden, since the meaning is: "Do not be present here, so that when you come I will not see you in it." As for the one who reads (mabsarah) with a fatha on the mim and the sad, its meaning is an intensification in describing the she-camel with clarity, like their saying: "The child is a source of cowardice (majbanah)."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But they wronged themselves by it⦆ Ibn 'Abbas said: they denied it. al-Akhfash said: their wrongdoing was with it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We send the signs only as a warning⦆; that is, We warn the servants so that they may take admonition.

The exegetes differ regarding what is meant by these signs, with four views:

One: they are the widespread death (al-mawt al-dhari'), related by al-Hasan. The second: the miracles of the messengers, which Allah made a means of warning to the deniers. The third: the signs of retribution as a warning against sins. The fourth: the alteration of a person's states from childhood to youth, then to middle age, then to old age, so that he may take a lesson from the change of his states and fear the outcome of his affair. Al-Mawardi mentioned these three views, and he attributed the last of them to our Imam Ahmad, may Allah be pleased with him.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 60:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when We said to you, "Indeed, your Lord has encompassed the people"﴾. On this there are three opinions:

First: His knowledge has encompassed the people. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Rabi' ibn Anas also said it. Muqatil said: His knowledge has encompassed the people, meaning the people of Makkah, that He would conquer it for His Messenger (ﷺ). (p-53)

Second: His power has encompassed the people, so they are in His grip. This was said by Mujahid.

Third: He prevented the people from killing you, so that you could convey His message. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people﴾. Regarding this vision there are two opinions:

One: It is a vision of the eye, which is what he saw on the night he was taken on the Night Journey (*isra'*) of wonders and signs. 'Ikrimah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: It is a vision of the eye which he saw on the night he was taken on the Night Journey. This meaning was adopted by al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, Masruq, al-Nakha'i, Qatadah, Abu Malik, Abu Salih, Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Zayd, and others. According to this view, the meaning of *fitnah* (trial) is testing, since some people believed what he said and others disbelieved. Ibn al-Anbari said: The preferred view regarding this vision is that it was while awake. There is no difference between one saying "I saw so-and-so with a *ru'yah*" and "I saw him with a *ru'ya*," except that *ru'yah* is used less often for a dream, while *ru'ya* is used more often for a dream; each of the two may be used in either sense.

Two: It is a vision of sleep. Within this there are two opinions. One: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had been shown that he would enter Makkah with his companions, while he was in Madinah at that time. He hastened before the appointed time, so the polytheists turned him back. Some people said: He has been turned back, but he had told us that he would enter it. So their turning back was their trial." This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. This does not contradict the hadith of the *mi'raj* (ascent), because this occurred in Madinah, while the *mi'raj* occurred in Makkah. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: Ibn 'Abbas mentioned it as an additional report to inform us that the polytheists in Makkah were tried by the vision of his eyes, and the hypocrites in Madinah were tried by the vision of his sleep. Two: He was shown the Banu Umayyah on pulpits, and this distressed him. He was told: They are only the worldly life that they will be given. Then he was comforted. Here *fitnah* means affliction. This was narrated by 'Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, although a report like this is not authentic, yet the majority of the exegetes have mentioned it.

Ibn al-Anbari narrated that Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw some people on pulpits, and this grieved him, and concerning this there was revealed: ﴿and the accursed tree in the Qur'an﴾." He said: The meaning of His saying ﴿except as a trial for the people﴾ is: except as an affliction for the people. Ibn al-Anbari said: Whoever holds that the tree refers to men whom the Prophet (ﷺ) saw in his sleep climbing the pulpits, argues that the tree is used as a metaphor for a woman because of its feminine grammatical gender, and for a group because its branches are gathered together. They said: The curse fell upon these people who were referred to by the tree. The exegetes said: In the verse there is inversion (*taqdim wa ta'khir*), its intended meaning being: We did not make the vision and the tree except as a trial for the people.

Regarding this tree there are three opinions:

One: It is the tree of Zaqqum. 'Ikrimah narrated it from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, 'Ikrimah, Masruq, al-Nakha'i, and the majority said the same. Muqatil said: When Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned the tree of Zaqqum, Abu Jahl said: "O assembly of Quraysh, Muhammad frightens you with the tree of Zaqqum. Do you not know that fire burns trees? Muhammad claims that fire grows trees! Do you know what Zaqqum is?" 'Abd Allah ibn al-Za'bara said: "Indeed, Zaqqum in the language of the Berbers is dates and butter." Abu Jahl said: "O slave-girl, bring us dates and butter!" She brought it to him, and he said to those around him: "Eat from this with which Muhammad frightens you!" So Allah, Exalted is He, revealed: ﴿And We frighten them, but it increases them only in great transgression﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: Their trial with the vision was their saying: "How can he go to Bayt al-Maqdis and return in one night?" And their trial with the tree was their saying: "How can there be a tree in the Fire?"

Regarding the meaning of ﴿accursed﴾ the scholars have three opinions: One: It is blameworthy, said by Ibn 'Abbas. Two: Its eater is cursed, mentioned by al-Zajjaj, who said: If there is no mention of its being cursed in the Qur'an, then it implies the cursing of those who eat it. He said: The Arabs say of every disgusting and harmful food: "accursed." As for His saying ﴿in the Qur'an﴾, the meaning is: the one that is mentioned in the Qur'an, and it is mentioned in His saying: ﴿Indeed, the tree of Zaqqum, the food of the sinful﴾ [al-Dukhan 44:43–44]. Three: The meaning of "accursed" is: removed far from the dwellings of the people of virtue; mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari. (p-56)

The second opinion: The accursed tree is that which twines around trees, meaning the dodder (*kashuth*), and this is also narrated from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: The tree is a metaphor for men, according to what we mentioned from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We frighten them﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: The object of "We frighten them" is omitted, its intended meaning being: and We frighten them with the punishment. ﴿But it increases them﴾, that is: the frightening only increases them ﴿in transgression﴾. We have already mentioned the meaning of *tughyan* (transgression) in (al-Baqarah 2:15), and we mentioned there the explanation of His saying: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," so they prostrated, except Iblis﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:34].

**Verse 61:** His words, Exalted is He: (آَسْجُدُ) ("Shall I prostrate?"). The Kufans read it with two hamzas, and the rest read it with one lengthened hamza. This is a rhetorical question of denial, meaning: "I would not do such a thing."

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Shall I prostrate myself before one whom You created from clay?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: "Ṭīnan" (clay) is in the accusative in two ways:

One: as a *tamyīz* (accusative of specification), meaning: "whom You created from clay." Two: as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative), meaning: "You brought him into being while he was made of clay." The phrase ﴿He said: Have you considered?﴾ (أرَأيْتَكَ) comes here without a conjunction, because the meaning is: "He said: 'Shall I prostrate before the one whom You created from clay? Have you considered?'" It means "Tell me." The *kāf* (you) is mentioned in address for emphasis. The answer is omitted, and the meaning is: "Tell me about this one whom You have honored over me. Why did You honor him over me, when You created me from fire and created him from clay?" The answer is omitted because the speech itself indicates it.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿If You give me respite until the Day of Resurrection﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read (أخَّرْتَنِي) with a *yā'* when connected. Ibn Kathir stopped on the *yā'*. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it without a *yā'*, both when connected and when stopping.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿I will surely seize control of his descendants﴾ (لأحْتَنِكَنَّ ذُرِّيَّتَهُ). There are three opinions:

One: "I will surely overpower them," said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Farra'. Two: "I will surely mislead them," said by Ibn Zayd. Three: "I will surely uproot them." It is said: "The locusts *iḥtanaka* what is on the earth," when they consume it, and "So-and-so *iḥtanaka* what another has of knowledge," when he exhausts it. The meaning is: "I will lead them wherever I wish." This is the opinion of Ibn Qutaybah.

If it is asked: "From where does he know the unseen?" we have answered this in the commentary on Surat al-Nisa' (4:119).

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Except a few﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: "They are the friends of Allah whom He protected."

**Verse 63:** His words, Exalted is He: ﴿He said: Go﴾ This expression includes granting him respite. ﴿Whoever follows you﴾, meaning: whoever follows your command from among them, that is, the descendants of Adam. *Al-mawfūr* means "the one made complete" (*al-muwaffir*). Ibn Qutaybah said: It is said "waffartu mālahu 'alayhi" and "wafartuhu," with light and heavy forms.

**Verse 64:** His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And incite whomever you can among them﴾ Ibn Qutaybah said: "Ist'akhiffa" (incite lightly). From this one says: "Istafazzanī fulān" (So-and-so provoked me).

Regarding the meaning of "His voice," there are two opinions: One: it is every caller who summons to disobedience of Allah, said by Ibn 'Abbas. Two: it is singing and musical instruments, said by Mujahid.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And rally against them﴾ (وَأجْلِبْ عَلَيْهِمْ), meaning: shout ﴿with your cavalry and your infantry﴾ and urge them against them by incitement. It is said: "Ajlaba al-qawm wa-jalabū" when they shouted. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: "Gather against them everything you can of your schemes." According to this, the *bā'* (in "with") is superfluous. Ibn Qutaybah said: *Al-rajl* means "the infantry" (*al-rajjāla*). It is said: "rājil" and "rajl," like "tājir" and "tajr," and "ṣāḥib" and "ṣaḥb." Ibn 'Abbas said: Every cavalry that travels in disobedience to Allah, and every man who travels in disobedience to Allah. Qatadah said: He has cavalry and infantry from the jinn and mankind.

Ḥafṣ related from 'Asim: (بِخَيْلِكَ ورَجِلِكَ) with a *kasra* on the *jīm*. This is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Razin, and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami. Abu Zayd said: It is said "rajulun rajil" for the one who walks on foot, and it is said "jā'anā ḥāfiyan rajulan" (he came to us barefoot, on foot). Ibn al-Sumayfa' and al-Jahdari read: (بِخَيْلِكَ ورُجّالِكَ) with a *ḍamma* on the *rā'*, a *shadda* on the *jīm* with a *fatḥa*, and an *alif* after it. Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu al-Jawza' and 'Ikrimah read: (ورِجالكَ) with a *kasra* on the *rā'* and a light *jīm* with an *alif*.

**Verse 64 (continued):** His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And share with them in wealth﴾ There are four opinions concerning it:

One: it is what they used to forbid of their livestock. This was narrated by 'Aṭiyyah from Ibn 'Abbas.

Two: wealth that was obtained unlawfully, said by Mujahid. Three: what they spent in acts of disobedience to Allah, said by al-Hasan. Four: what they slaughtered for their idols, said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

As for his sharing with them in children, there are four opinions concerning it:

One: they are illegitimate children (children of fornication). This was narrated by 'Aṭiyyah from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said the same.

Two: the infants buried alive (*al-mawūdah*) from among their children. This was narrated by 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas.

Three: it is their naming of their children as slaves to their idols, such as 'Abd Shams, 'Abd al-'Uzzā, and 'Abd Manāf. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

Four: what they circumcised (*majjasū*, marking them as Magians), Judaized, Christianized, and dyed of their children with a dye other than the dye of Islam. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

**Verse 64 (continued):** His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And promise them﴾ We have already mentioned it in His words: ﴿He promises them and gives them hope…﴾ up to the end of the verse (4:120). This verse is phrased as a command, but its meaning is a threat. An example of this in speech is that you say to a person: "Exert your utmost effort, and you will see what will befall you." Al-Zajjaj said: When a command is preceded by a prohibition against what is commanded, its meaning is threat and warning. You say to a man: "Do not enter this house," and when he attempts to enter it you say: "Enter it, if you are a man." You are not commanding him to enter, but you are warning and threatening him. A similar example is: ﴿Do what you wish﴾ (41:40), though they were forbidden to do acts of disobedience. Ibn al-Anbari said: This is a command whose meaning is threat. Its implied meaning is: "If you do this, We will punish you and torment you." It was shifted from the form of a conditional to the form of a command, like His words: ﴿Whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ (18:29).

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ We have explained it in the commentary on Surat al-Ḥijr (15:42).

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And sufficient is your Lord as a Guardian﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: He is sufficient as a Guardian for His allies, protecting them from accepting anything from Iblis.

**Verse 64:** His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And incite whomever you can among them﴾ Ibn Qutaybah said: "Ist'akhiffa" (incite lightly). From this one says: "Istafazzanī fulān" (So-and-so provoked me).

Regarding the meaning of "His voice," there are two opinions: One: it is every caller who summons to disobedience of Allah, said by Ibn 'Abbas. Two: it is singing and musical instruments, said by Mujahid.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And rally against them﴾ (وَأجْلِبْ عَلَيْهِمْ), meaning: shout ﴿with your cavalry and your infantry﴾ and urge them against them by incitement. It is said: "Ajlaba al-qawm wa-jalabū" when they shouted. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: "Gather against them everything you can of your schemes." According to this, the *bā'* (in "with") is superfluous. Ibn Qutaybah said: *Al-rajl* means "the infantry" (*al-rajjāla*). It is said: "rājil" and "rajl," like "tājir" and "tajr," and "ṣāḥib" and "ṣaḥb." Ibn 'Abbas said: Every cavalry that travels in disobedience to Allah, and every man who travels in disobedience to Allah. Qatadah said: He has cavalry and infantry from the jinn and mankind.

Ḥafṣ related from 'Asim: (بِخَيْلِكَ ورَجِلِكَ) with a *kasra* on the *jīm*. This is the reading of Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Razin, and Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami. Abu Zayd said: It is said "rajulun rajil" for the one who walks on foot, and it is said "jā'anā ḥāfiyan rajulan" (he came to us barefoot, on foot). Ibn al-Sumayfa' and al-Jahdari read: (بِخَيْلِكَ ورُجّالِكَ) with a *ḍamma* on the *rā'*, a *shadda* on the *jīm* with a *fatḥa*, and an *alif* after it. Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu al-Jawza' and 'Ikrimah read: (ورِجالكَ) with a *kasra* on the *rā'* and a light *jīm* with an *alif*.

**Verse 64 (continued):** His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And share with them in wealth﴾ There are four opinions concerning it:

One: it is what they used to forbid of their livestock. This was narrated by 'Aṭiyyah from Ibn 'Abbas.

Two: wealth that was obtained unlawfully, said by Mujahid. Three: what they spent in acts of disobedience to Allah, said by al-Hasan. Four: what they slaughtered for their idols, said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

As for his sharing with them in children, there are four opinions concerning it:

One: they are illegitimate children (children of fornication). This was narrated by 'Aṭiyyah from Ibn 'Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid and al-Ḍaḥḥāk said the same.

Two: the infants buried alive (*al-mawūdah*) from among their children. This was narrated by 'Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas.

Three: it is their naming of their children as slaves to their idols, such as 'Abd Shams, 'Abd al-'Uzzā, and 'Abd Manāf. This was narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

Four: what they circumcised (*majjasū*, marking them as Magians), Judaized, Christianized, and dyed of their children with a dye other than the dye of Islam. This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

**Verse 64 (continued):** His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And promise them﴾ We have already mentioned it in His words: ﴿He promises them and gives them hope…﴾ up to the end of the verse (4:120). This verse is phrased as a command, but its meaning is a threat. An example of this in speech is that you say to a person: "Exert your utmost effort, and you will see what will befall you." Al-Zajjaj said: When a command is preceded by a prohibition against what is commanded, its meaning is threat and warning. You say to a man: "Do not enter this house," and when he attempts to enter it you say: "Enter it, if you are a man." You are not commanding him to enter, but you are warning and threatening him. A similar example is: ﴿Do what you wish﴾ (41:40), though they were forbidden to do acts of disobedience. Ibn al-Anbari said: This is a command whose meaning is threat. Its implied meaning is: "If you do this, We will punish you and torment you." It was shifted from the form of a conditional to the form of a command, like His words: ﴿Whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ (18:29).

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them﴾ We have explained it in the commentary on Surat al-Ḥijr (15:42).

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And sufficient is your Lord as a Guardian﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: He is sufficient as a Guardian for His allies, protecting them from accepting anything from Iblis.

**Verse 61:** His words, Exalted is He: (آَسْجُدُ) ("Shall I prostrate?"). The Kufans read it with two hamzas, and the rest read it with one lengthened hamza. This is a rhetorical question of denial, meaning: "I would not do such a thing."

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Shall I prostrate myself before one whom You created from clay?﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: "Ṭīnan" (clay) is in the accusative in two ways:

One: as a *tamyīz* (accusative of specification), meaning: "whom You created from clay." Two: as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative), meaning: "You brought him into being while he was made of clay." The phrase ﴿He said: Have you considered?﴾ (أرَأيْتَكَ) comes here without a conjunction, because the meaning is: "He said: 'Shall I prostrate before the one whom You created from clay? Have you considered?'" It means "Tell me." The *kāf* (you) is mentioned in address for emphasis. The answer is omitted, and the meaning is: "Tell me about this one whom You have honored over me. Why did You honor him over me, when You created me from fire and created him from clay?" The answer is omitted because the speech itself indicates it.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿If You give me respite until the Day of Resurrection﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read (أخَّرْتَنِي) with a *yā'* when connected. Ibn Kathir stopped on the *yā'*. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it without a *yā'*, both when connected and when stopping.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿I will surely seize control of his descendants﴾ (لأحْتَنِكَنَّ ذُرِّيَّتَهُ). There are three opinions:

One: "I will surely overpower them," said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Farra'. Two: "I will surely mislead them," said by Ibn Zayd. Three: "I will surely uproot them." It is said: "The locusts *iḥtanaka* what is on the earth," when they consume it, and "So-and-so *iḥtanaka* what another has of knowledge," when he exhausts it. The meaning is: "I will lead them wherever I wish." This is the opinion of Ibn Qutaybah.

If it is asked: "From where does he know the unseen?" we have answered this in the commentary on Surat al-Nisa' (4:119).

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿Except a few﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: "They are the friends of Allah whom He protected."

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verses 66–70:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Your Lord is the One who drives for you the ships﴾; that is, He makes them run. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said, "zajaytu al-shay'," meaning I pushed the thing forward.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that you may seek of His bounty﴾; that is, in seeking trade.

Regarding "min" (from) there are three views:

The first: it is extra (ziyadah). The second: it is partitive (lil-tab'id). The third: the object is omitted, and the sense is: "that you may seek from His bounty the provision and the good," as Ibn al-Anbari mentioned.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed He is ever Merciful to you﴾. This address is specific to the believers. Then He addressed the polytheists, saying: ﴿And when harm touches you at sea﴾, meaning the fear of drowning, ﴿those whom you call upon fade away (p-61)﴾; that is, those whom you call upon of the deities go astray, except Allah, Exalted is He. It is said that "dalla" here means "ghaba" (disappeared); it is said, "dalla al-ma' fi al-laban" when the water vanishes into the milk. The meaning is: you sincerely directed your supplication to Allah and forgot the rivals. Mujahid and Abu al-Mutawakkil read (ḍalla man yad'una) with the yā' (i.e., "yaḍillu," with the verb in the masculine third-person form and the "y" prefix). ﴿But when He brings you safely to land, you turn away﴾ from faith and sincerity; ﴿and man has ever been ungrateful﴾, meaning the disbelieving human, ﴿ungrateful﴾ for the blessing of his Lord.

﴿Do you then feel secure﴾ when you have come out of the sea ﴿that He will cause you to sink into the side of the land﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read (nakhsifu bikum, aw nursila, an nu'idakum, fa-nursila, fa-nughriqukum) with the nūn throughout. Nafi', Asim, Ibn Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read with the yā' throughout. The meaning of "nakhsifu bikum janiba al-barr" is: We will make you disappear and take you away into a region of the land. The meaning is that My command is effective on land just as its effect is on the sea.

"Or He will send upon you a hasiban (violent wind)": regarding this there are three views:

The first: that "al-ḥāṣib" is stones from the sky; this was said by Qatadah.

The second: that it is a violent wind that pelts with pebbles. This was said by Abu Ubaydah, who cited the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"Facing the north wind, it strikes them
with a hasib like scattered cotton fluff."

Ibn Qutaybah said: "al-ḥāṣib" is the wind, so named because it pelts (taḥṣibu), that is, throws small pebbles (al-ḥaṣbā'), which are small stones. Ibn al-Anbari said: The philologists say: "al-ḥāṣib" is the wind in which there are pebbles. He said: The reason why it is said "ḥāṣiban" of the wind and not "ḥāṣibah" is that it is an attribute that is specific to the wind, and it had no masculine form to which it could shift in some circumstance; so it is like their saying "ḥā'iḍ" (menstruating) of a woman, since they do not say "rajul ḥā'iḍ" (a menstruating man). He said: There is another answer as well (p-62): that the adjective of the wind is stripped of the feminine marker, so it resembles masculine nouns in this respect, just as they say "al-samā' amṭara" (the sky rained) and "al-arḍ anbata" (the earth grew).

The third: that "al-ḥāṣib" is dust in which there are pebbles. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then you would not find for yourselves any disposer of affairs﴾; that is, any preventer or helper.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or do you feel secure that He will return you into it﴾; that is, into the sea ﴿at another time﴾; that is, once again. The plural is "tārāt." ﴿Then send upon you a violent wind that will destroy you﴾. Abu Ubaydah said: It is the wind that breaks everything. Ibn Qutaybah said: "al-qāṣif" is the wind [that] breaks trees; that is, that breaks them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and drown you﴾. Abu al-Mutawakkil, [Abu] Ja'far, Shaybah and Ruways read (fa-tughriqukum) with the tā' (t), with a sukūn on the ghayn and a light rā'. Abu al-Jawza' and Ayyub read (fa-yughharriqukum) with the yā', with a fatḥah on the ghayn and a shaddah on it. Abu Raja' read like this, except with the tā'. ﴿Because you disbelieved﴾; that is, because of your disbelief, when you were saved the first time. ﴿Then you would not find for yourselves against Us any avenger for it.﴾ Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, who would pursue on account of your blood; that is, would demand [retribution] from us.

Abdullah ibn Amr, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: The winds of punishment are four: two on land and two at sea. The two on land are the ṣarṣar and the ʿaqīm; the two at sea are the ʿāṣif and the qāṣif.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have honoured the children of Adam﴾; that is, We preferred them. Abu Ubaydah said: "karramnā" is more intensive than "akramnā."

Regarding that by which they were preferred, the commentators have eleven views:

The first: they were preferred over all creation except a group of the angels: Jibril, Mikail, Israfil, the Angel of Death, and their like. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. (p-63) According to this, the intended meaning is the believers among them, and their preference is by faith.

The second: all other animals eat with their mouths, except the son of Adam, who eats with his hand. This was narrated by Maymun ibn Mihran from Ibn Abbas. Some commentators said: the intended meaning of this preference is that they eat with their hands and that what they eat is clean, since the jinn feed on bones and dung.

The third: they were preferred by intellect. This was narrated from Ibn Abbas.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verses 66–70:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Your Lord is the One who drives for you the ships﴾; that is, He makes them run. Al-Zajjaj said: It is said, "zajaytu al-shay'," meaning I pushed the thing forward.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that you may seek of His bounty﴾; that is, in seeking trade.

Regarding "min" (from) there are three views:

The first: it is extra (ziyadah). The second: it is partitive (lil-tab'id). The third: the object is omitted, and the sense is: "that you may seek from His bounty the provision and the good," as Ibn al-Anbari mentioned.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed He is ever Merciful to you﴾. This address is specific to the believers. Then He addressed the polytheists, saying: ﴿And when harm touches you at sea﴾, meaning the fear of drowning, ﴿those whom you call upon fade away (p-61)﴾; that is, those whom you call upon of the deities go astray, except Allah, Exalted is He. It is said that "dalla" here means "ghaba" (disappeared); it is said, "dalla al-ma' fi al-laban" when the water vanishes into the milk. The meaning is: you sincerely directed your supplication to Allah and forgot the rivals. Mujahid and Abu al-Mutawakkil read (ḍalla man yad'una) with the yā' (i.e., "yaḍillu," with the verb in the masculine third-person form and the "y" prefix). ﴿But when He brings you safely to land, you turn away﴾ from faith and sincerity; ﴿and man has ever been ungrateful﴾, meaning the disbelieving human, ﴿ungrateful﴾ for the blessing of his Lord.

﴿Do you then feel secure﴾ when you have come out of the sea ﴿that He will cause you to sink into the side of the land﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read (nakhsifu bikum, aw nursila, an nu'idakum, fa-nursila, fa-nughriqukum) with the nūn throughout. Nafi', Asim, Ibn Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read with the yā' throughout. The meaning of "nakhsifu bikum janiba al-barr" is: We will make you disappear and take you away into a region of the land. The meaning is that My command is effective on land just as its effect is on the sea.

"Or He will send upon you a hasiban (violent wind)": regarding this there are three views:

The first: that "al-ḥāṣib" is stones from the sky; this was said by Qatadah.

The second: that it is a violent wind that pelts with pebbles. This was said by Abu Ubaydah, who cited the verse of al-Farazdaq:

"Facing the north wind, it strikes them
with a hasib like scattered cotton fluff."

Ibn Qutaybah said: "al-ḥāṣib" is the wind, so named because it pelts (taḥṣibu), that is, throws small pebbles (al-ḥaṣbā'), which are small stones. Ibn al-Anbari said: The philologists say: "al-ḥāṣib" is the wind in which there are pebbles. He said: The reason why it is said "ḥāṣiban" of the wind and not "ḥāṣibah" is that it is an attribute that is specific to the wind, and it had no masculine form to which it could shift in some circumstance; so it is like their saying "ḥā'iḍ" (menstruating) of a woman, since they do not say "rajul ḥā'iḍ" (a menstruating man). He said: There is another answer as well (p-62): that the adjective of the wind is stripped of the feminine marker, so it resembles masculine nouns in this respect, just as they say "al-samā' amṭara" (the sky rained) and "al-arḍ anbata" (the earth grew).

The third: that "al-ḥāṣib" is dust in which there are pebbles. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then you would not find for yourselves any disposer of affairs﴾; that is, any preventer or helper.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Or do you feel secure that He will return you into it﴾; that is, into the sea ﴿at another time﴾; that is, once again. The plural is "tārāt." ﴿Then send upon you a violent wind that will destroy you﴾. Abu Ubaydah said: It is the wind that breaks everything. Ibn Qutaybah said: "al-qāṣif" is the wind [that] breaks trees; that is, that breaks them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and drown you﴾. Abu al-Mutawakkil, [Abu] Ja'far, Shaybah and Ruways read (fa-tughriqukum) with the tā' (t), with a sukūn on the ghayn and a light rā'. Abu al-Jawza' and Ayyub read (fa-yughharriqukum) with the yā', with a fatḥah on the ghayn and a shaddah on it. Abu Raja' read like this, except with the tā'. ﴿Because you disbelieved﴾; that is, because of your disbelief, when you were saved the first time. ﴿Then you would not find for yourselves against Us any avenger for it.﴾ Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, who would pursue on account of your blood; that is, would demand [retribution] from us.

Abdullah ibn Amr, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: The winds of punishment are four: two on land and two at sea. The two on land are the ṣarṣar and the ʿaqīm; the two at sea are the ʿāṣif and the qāṣif.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have honoured the children of Adam﴾; that is, We preferred them. Abu Ubaydah said: "karramnā" is more intensive than "akramnā."

Regarding that by which they were preferred, the commentators have eleven views:

The first: they were preferred over all creation except a group of the angels: Jibril, Mikail, Israfil, the Angel of Death, and their like. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. (p-63) According to this, the intended meaning is the believers among them, and their preference is by faith.

The second: all other animals eat with their mouths, except the son of Adam, who eats with his hand. This was narrated by Maymun ibn Mihran from Ibn Abbas. Some commentators said: the intended meaning of this preference is that they eat with their hands and that what they eat is clean, since the jinn feed on bones and dung.

The third: they were preferred by intellect. This was narrated from Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: by speech and discernment. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The fifth: by the balance and extension of stature. This was said by Ata'.

The sixth: by making Muhammad (ﷺ) one of them. This was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

The seventh: they were preferred by food and pleasures in this world. This was said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

The eighth: by beauty of form. This was said by Yaman.

The ninth: by their dominion over other creatures and the subjugation of all creation to them. This was said by Muhammad ibn Jarir.

The tenth: by command and prohibition. Al-Mawardi mentioned it.

The eleventh: by the beard being for men and the locks of hair for women. Al-Tha'labi mentioned it.

If it is said: How can the mention of honour be applied to all of them, when among them is the disbelieving despised one?

The answer is from two aspects: The first: that He treated all of them as those honoured with abundant blessings. The second: that since among them there were those with this attribute, the attribute was applied to their whole group, as in His saying: ﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾ [Al 'Imran: 110].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We carried them on land﴾, upon moist livers, which are: camels, horses, mules and donkeys; and ﴿on the sea﴾, upon dry planks, which are: ships. ﴿And We provided them with good things﴾; regarding this there are two views:

The first: the lawful. The second: what is pleasant to the taste.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We preferred them over many of those We have created with [definite] preference﴾. Regarding this there are two views:

The first: that it is to be taken literally, and that they were not preferred over all created beings. We have mentioned (p-64) from Ibn Abbas that they were preferred over all creation except a group of the angels, and others said: rather, the angels are more excellent.

The second: that its meaning is: and We preferred them over all of those We have created. The Arabs place "al-akthar" and "al-kathir" in the position of the plural, as in His saying: ﴿They listen eagerly, and most of them are liars﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 223]. Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "The believer is more honoured by Allah, Mighty and Majestic, than the angels who are with Him."

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 17, verses 71–72:**

Allah's words: ﴿The day We shall call together every people with their leader﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative (منصوب, *manṣūb*) on the sense of "remember" (اذْكُرْ, *udhkur*), that is, "[Remember] the day We call every people…" The intended meaning is the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Hasan al-Basri read يَوْمَ يَدْعُو (*yawma yad'ū*) with a ya, and كُلَّ (*kulla*) in the accusative. Abu 'Imran al-Jawni read يَوْمَ يُدْعى (*yawma yud'ā*) with a raised ya and a fatha on the 'ayn followed by an alif, and كُلُّ (*kullu*) in the nominative.

As for what is meant by "their leader" (بِإِمَامِهِمْ, *bi-imāmihim*), there are four opinions:

The first: it is their chief. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated from him that he said: it is either a leader of guidance or a leader of misguidance.

The second: it is their deeds. This was narrated by 'Atiyya from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliya also said this.

The third: it is their prophet. This was said by Anas ibn Malik, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatada, and, in one narration, Mujahid.

The fourth: it is their book. This was said by 'Ikrima and, in one narration, Mujahid. Then there are two views on this. One: it is the book in which their deeds are recorded; this was said by Qatada and Muqatil. The other: it is the book revealed to them; this was said by al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd.

According to the first view, it is said: "O followers of Musa, O followers of 'Isa, O followers of Muhammad (ﷺ)," and it may also be said: "O followers of the leaders of misguidance." According to the second: "O you who did such and such." According to the third: "O nation of Musa, O nation of 'Isa, O nation of Muhammad (ﷺ)." According to the fourth: "O People of the Torah, O People of the Gospel, O People of the Qur'an," or "O owner of the book in which he did such and such."

Allah's words: ﴿Then those will read their record﴾. Its meaning: they will read their good deeds, because they took their books in their right hands through their faith.

Allah's words: ﴿and they will not be wronged a fatil﴾; that is, they will not be deprived of their reward by the amount of a fatil (فَتِيل, *fatīl*, the thread in a date-stone). We have explained this in Surah al-Nisa' (4:49).

Allah's words: ﴿And whoever is blind in this [world]﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Ibn 'Amir read أَعْمَى فَهُوَ فِي الْآخِرَةِ أَعْمَى (*a'mā fa-huwa fī al-ākhirati a'mā*) with fatha on the mim in both places. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read both with kasra on the mim. Abu 'Amr read فِي هَذِهِ أَعْمَى (*fī hādhihi a'mā*) with kasra on the mim, and فَهُوَ فِي الْآخِرَةِ أَعْمَى (*fa-huwa fī al-ākhirati a'mā*) with fatha on it.

As for what is referred to by "this" (هَذِهِ, *hādhihi*), there are two views:

The first: it is the present world (الدُّنْيا, *al-dunyā*). This was said by Mujahid. Then there are five opinions on the meaning of the statement:
One: whoever is blind in this world to knowledge of Allah's power in creating things, will be blind to what is described to him about the Hereafter. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.
Two: whoever is blind in this world through disbelief, will be blind in the Hereafter, because in this world his repentance is accepted, but in the Hereafter it is not. This was said by al-Hasan.
Three: whoever is blind to the signs of Allah in this world, is blinder regarding what is hidden from him of the matters of the Hereafter.
Four: whoever is blind to the blessings of Allah which He explained in His words: ﴿Your Lord is He who drives for you the ship in the sea…﴾ until His words: ﴿…preferred﴾, then he will be blind in the Hereafter to his right guidance and well-being. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned these two opinions.
Five: whoever is blind to the proof in it, will be blind in the Hereafter to Paradise. This was said by Abu Bakr al-Warraq.

The second: it refers to the blessings (النِّعَمُ, *ni'am*). Then there are two views on the statement:
One: whoever is blind to the blessings that are seen and witnessed, will be blind in the Hereafter which is not seen. This was narrated by 'Ikrima from Ibn 'Abbas.
The other: whoever is blind to knowing the right of Allah in these blessings mentioned in His words: ﴿And We have certainly honored the children of Adam﴾, and does not give thanks for them, then he is blind in what lies between him and Allah of what would bring him nearer to Him, ﴿and more astray in way﴾. This was said by al-Suddi.

Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the meaning of His words ﴿in the Hereafter is blind﴾ is "more blind" (أَشَدُّ عَمًى, *ashaddu 'aman*), because in this world it was possible for him to leave his blindness through reasoning, but in the Hereafter there is no way for him to leave his blindness. It was also said: the meaning of blindness in the Hereafter is that he will not be guided to the path of reward. All of this is blindness of the heart.

If it is asked: why did He say ﴿so he in the Hereafter is blind﴾, and did not say "more blind" (أَشَدُّ عَمًى)? Because blindness is a natural condition, like redness and blueness, and the Arabs say: "How intense is Zayd's blackness!" and "How clear is 'Amr's blueness!" but they rarely say: "How black is Zayd!" or "How blue is 'Amr!"

The answer: the intended blindness here is blindness of the heart, and that increases, and something new arises from it step by step, which differs from the inherent natural conditions that do not increase, such as blindness of the eye, whiteness, and redness. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned this.
