[p. 68]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And indeed they nearly tempted you away from that which We revealed to you﴾. There are four reports about the occasion of its revelation:

The first: "A delegation from Thaqif came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'Grant us the benefit of al-Lat for a year, and make our valley sacred as you made Makkah sacred.' He refused. They kept pressing their request and said: 'We would like you to let the Arabs know our superiority over them. If you fear that the Arabs will say, "You gave them what you did not give us," then say, "Allah commanded me to do so."' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) [held back from them], and greed took hold of them, and this verse was revealed." Ata' narrated it from Ibn Abbas. Ata'iyyah narrated from Ibn Abbas that they said: "Give us a year's respite; then we will submit and break our idols." He was inclined to grant them the respite, and this verse was revealed.

The second: "The polytheists said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'We will not leave you alone unless you touch our gods, even with the tips of your fingers.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'What harm is there if I did, and Allah knows that I am averse to it?' Then this verse was revealed." Sa'id ibn Jubayr said this. But this is false: it is not permissible to attribute it to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), nor is what we mentioned from Ata'iyyah, that he was inclined to grant them a year's respite. All of this is impossible concerning him, and concerning the Companions, who narrated from him.

The third: "The Quraysh spent a night with the Messenger of Allah until morning, speaking to him and exalting him, saying: 'You are our chief and the son of our chief.' They kept at him until he nearly approached them in some of what they wanted. Then Allah protected him from that, and this verse was revealed." Qatadah said this.

The fourth: "They said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): 'Drive away from yourself the rabble and their clients, those whose smell is like that of sheep, because they wear wool. Then we will sit with you and listen to you.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was inclined to do what would invite their Islam, and these verses were revealed." Al-Zajjaj related this and said: The meaning of the speech is "they nearly tempted you," and "inna" and the "lam" are for emphasis. The commentators said: He said ﴿would tempt you﴾ because granting them what they asked would contradict the ruling of the Qur'an.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿to fabricate against Us other than it﴾, that is, to invent [something] against Us, which is their saying: "Say, 'Allah commanded me to do so.'" ﴿And then they would have taken you as a friend﴾, that is, they would have allied with you and befriended you.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And had We not given you firmness﴾ upon the truth, by Our protecting you, ﴿you would have almost inclined toward them﴾, that is, you were inclined and nearly moved toward their desire ﴿a little.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: "That was when you remained silent in answer to them, and Allah knows best His intention." Ibn al-Anbari said: The verb is outwardly directed at the Prophet (ﷺ) but inwardly at the polytheists, and its implied sense is: "They nearly made you incline toward them, and attributed to you what they desired, which you dislike." He attributed the verb to other than its doer when there was no risk of confusion, as a man says to another: "You nearly killed yourself today," meaning: "You nearly did an act by which someone else would kill you." This is [a case of] figurative usage (majaz) and extended usage (ittisa'). Similar to this is His saying: ﴿So do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 132), and the speaker's saying: "I will not see you in this place."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] in life and double [punishment] in death.﴾ The meaning: If you had done that small thing, ﴿We would have made you taste double in life﴾, that is, double the punishment of life, ﴿and double﴾ punishment ﴿in death﴾. A similar line is the poet's:

"I was told that the fire was kindled after you,
and after you, O Kulayb, the assembly fell to abuse."

That is, the people of the assembly. Ibn Abbas said: "Double the punishment of this world and the Hereafter." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was protected, but this is a warning to his community, so that none of the believers would incline toward any of the polytheists in any matter of Allah's rulings and laws.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And indeed they nearly drove you out of the land﴾. There are two reports about the occasion of its revelation:

The first: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived in Madinah, the Jews envied him for his standing in Madinah and disliked his nearness. They came to him and said: 'O Muhammad, are you a prophet?' He said: 'Yes.' They said: 'By Allah, you know that this is not the land of the prophets, and that the land of the prophets is al-Sham. So if you are a prophet, go to al-Sham.' Then this verse was revealed." Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn Abbas. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was determined to leave Madinah, and this verse was revealed. [p. 70] Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm said: When the Jews said this to him, he accepted what they said, and he undertook the expedition of Tabuk intending nothing but al-Sham. When he reached Tabuk, this verse was revealed.

The second: They were the polytheists, the people of Makkah, who planned to expel the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from Makkah, so Allah commanded him to leave, and revealed this verse informing of what they had planned. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said this. Qatadah said: They were the people of Makkah, [who intended] to expel him from Makkah; had they done so, they would not have been given respite, but Allah restrained them from expelling him until He commanded him to leave. It was also said: They did not remain [long] until Allah sent death upon them at Badr.

According to the first view, the ones referred to are the Jews, and "the land" is Madinah. According to the second, they are the polytheists, and "the land" is Makkah. The meaning of "al-istifzaz" (driving out) has already been mentioned earlier (Al-Isra: 64). Similar to this is His saying: ﴿So do not die except while you are Muslims﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 132), and the speaker's saying: "I will not see you in this place."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] in life and double [punishment] in death.﴾ The meaning: If you had done that small thing, ﴿We would have made you taste double in life﴾, that is, double the punishment of life, ﴿and double﴾ punishment ﴿in death﴾. A similar line is the poet's:

"I was told that the fire was kindled after you,
and after you, O Kulayb, the assembly fell to abuse."

That is, the people of the assembly. Ibn Abbas said: "Double the punishment of this world and the Hereafter." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was protected, but this is a warning to his community, so that none of the believers would incline toward any of the polytheists in any matter of Allah's rulings and laws.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And indeed they nearly drove you out of the land﴾. There are two reports about the occasion of its revelation:

The first: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived in Madinah, the Jews envied him for his standing in Madinah and disliked his nearness. They came to him and said: 'O Muhammad, are you a prophet?' He said: 'Yes.' They said: 'By Allah, you know that this is not the land of the prophets, and that the land of the prophets is al-Sham. So if you are a prophet, go to al-Sham.' Then this verse was revealed." Abu Salih narrated it from Ibn Abbas. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was determined to leave Madinah, and this verse was revealed. [p. 70] Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm said: When the Jews said this to him, he accepted what they said, and he undertook the expedition of Tabuk intending nothing but al-Sham. When he reached Tabuk, this verse was revealed.

The second: They were the polytheists, the people of Makkah, who planned to expel the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from Makkah, so Allah commanded him to leave, and revealed this verse informing of what they had planned. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said this. Qatadah said: They were the people of Makkah, [who intended] to expel him from Makkah; had they done so, they would not have been given respite, but Allah restrained them from expelling him until He commanded him to leave. It was also said: They did not remain [long] until Allah sent death upon them at Badr.

According to the first view, the ones referred to are the Jews, and "the land" is Madinah. According to the second, they are the polytheists, and "the land" is Makkah. The meaning of "al-istifzaz" (driving out) has already been mentioned earlier (Al-Isra: 64). It was also said that what is meant here is killing, so that they would drive him out of the whole land; this was reported from al-Hasan.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And then they would not have remained after you except a little.﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "khalfaka" (after you). Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read "khilafaka" (after you / in opposition to you). Al-Akhfash said: "Khilafaka" has the meaning of "khalfaka," and the meaning is: they would not remain after your departure ﴿except a little﴾, that is: had they driven you out, We would have destroyed them shortly after your departure. Allah repaid them for what they planned: He killed the chiefs of the polytheists at Badr, killed the Banu Qurayzah from among the Jews, and expelled the Banu al-Nadir. Ibn al-Anbari said: The meaning of the speech is: "They would not remain [in] opposition to you and defiance of you," so the preposition (harf al-khafd) was dropped. Abu Razin and Abu al-Mutawakkil read "khilafaka" with a damma on the kha', a shadda on the lam, and a raf' on the fa'.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿[as] the way of those We sent before you﴾. Al-Farra' said: "Sunnah" is put in the accusative by an implied verb of punishment, meaning: they will be punished according to Our way concerning those We sent. Al-Akhfash said: The meaning is: He established it as a way. Al-Zajjaj said: The accusative is in the sense of ﴿would not remain﴾, and its interpretation is: We have established this way concerning those We sent before you, that when they expel their prophet or kill him, punishment does not delay in descending upon them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 78–81:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Establish the prayer﴾; i.e., perform it, ﴿at the decline of the sun﴾; i.e., at its declining. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned two opinions regarding the lam (in li-dulūki): first, that it means "in" (fī). Second, that it is emphatic (muʾakkadah), like His saying ﴿It has followed closely upon you﴾ [An-Naml: 72]. Abu ʿUbayda said: its dulūk is from the time of its zawal (passing of the meridian) until it sets. Al-Zajjaj said: its inclination at midday is dulūk, and its inclination toward sunset is dulūk. Al-Azhari said: the meaning of al-dulūk (declining) in the speech of the Arabs is zawal (decline/passing), and for this reason the sun, when it passes the middle of the day, is called dālikah, and when it sets, it is called dālikah, because in both states it is declining.

Regarding the intended meaning of dulūk here, the commentators have two opinions:

First: that it is its zawal at midday. Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated: "I invited the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and whomever of his companions he wished, and they ate at my place. Then they went out when the sun had passed its zenith, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out and said: 'Go out, O Abu Bakr, for this is when the sun declines (dalakat al-shams).'" This is the view of Ibn ʿUmar, Abu Barzah, Abu Hurayrah, al-Hasan, al-Shaʿbi, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Abu al-ʿAliyah, Mujahid, ʿAta', ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, and Muqatil, and it is the choice of al-Azhari. Al-Azhari said: so that the verse encompasses the five prayers, the meaning being: "Establish the prayer from the time of the sun's zawal until the darkness of the night (ghasaq al-layl)," which includes the Dhuhr, the ʿAsr, and the two prayers of the darkness of the night, which are the ʿIshaʾs; then He said: ﴿and the Qurʾan of dawn﴾, and so these are five prayers.

Second: that it is its setting. This was said by Ibn Masʿud, al-Nakhaʿi, and Ibn Zayd, and from Ibn ʿAbbas there are two reports similar to the two opinions. Al-Farraʾ said: I have seen the Arabs understand dulūk as the disappearance of the sun, and this is the choice of Ibn Qutaybah. He said: because the Arabs say: "the star declined (dalaka al-najm)" when it set. Dhu al-Rummah said:

Lamps that are not led by the stars (nujūm) nor by the setting ones (al-afilāt al-dawālik)

And they say of the sun: "dalakat bi-rāḥ," meaning it set, while the observer has placed his palm on his brow looking at it. A poet said:

And the sun has nearly become a sick one, / I push it with wine that it may slip away

He likened it to the sick man in his final illness (danaf), because it was about to set, just as death approaches the one in the final illness. The observer looks at it from beneath the palm only to know how much remains for it until it sets, and to shield the rays with his hand. Accordingly, on this view the prayer intended is the Maghrib. As for the darkness of the night (ghasaq al-layl), it is its darkness.

Regarding the intended prayer connected with the darkness of the night, there are three opinions: First: the ʿIshaʾ, said by Ibn Masʿud. Second: the Maghrib, said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Qadi Abu Yaʿla said: it is possible that the intended meaning is clarifying the time of the Maghrib, that it runs from the sun's setting until the darkness of the night. Third: the Maghrib and the ʿIshaʾ, said by al-Hasan.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and the Qurʾan of dawn﴾ means: and establish the recitation of dawn. The commentators said: what is intended by it is the Fajr prayer. Al-Zajjaj said: in this there is a great benefit, indicating that the prayer is not except with recitation, since the prayer has been called "Qurʾan."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the Qurʾan of dawn is ever witnessed﴾. Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "The angels of the night and the angels of the day witness it."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And from the night, pray Tahajjud with it﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: pray with the Qurʾan. Mujahid, ʿAlqamah, and al-Aswad said: tahajjud is after sleep. Ibn Qutaybah said: tahajjadtu means I stayed awake, and hajadtu means I slept. Ibn al-Anbari said: tahajjud here means alertness and wakefulness, and the lexicographers say it is one of the words with opposite meanings: it is said of the sleeper: hājid and mutahajjid, and likewise of the one who stays awake. al-Nabighah said:

Even if she appeared to a white-haired monk, a servant of God, a celibate, mutahajjid

We would be amazed at her beauty and the sweetness of her speech, and at her mole, though he would not be rightly guided

By al-mutahajjid he means the one who stays awake. Labid said:

He said: "We have slept, for the night has grown long, / and we have been able, if we were heedless of time..."

That is, "he put us to sleep." Al-Azhari said: al-mutahajjid is one who rises from sleep to prayer. It was said of him: mutahajjid, because he casts off drowsiness (hujūd) from himself, just as one says: taharraja and ta'ththama (he avoided sin and acted sinfully).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿as a supererogatory (nāfilah) for you﴾. Nāfilah in the language means what is in excess of the basic obligation.

Regarding the meaning of this excess in his case, there are two opinions:

First: that it is an addition to what was obligated upon him, so the meaning is: an obligation upon you. The qiyam al-layl was obligatory upon him. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

Second: that it is an addition beyond the obligation and is not obligatory; the meaning is: voluntary and virtuous. Abu Umamah, al-Hasan, and Mujahid said: the nāfilah is for the Prophet ﷺ alone. Mujahid said: this is because his past and future sins have been forgiven, so whatever exceeds his obligation is a supererogatory and a virtue for him, while for others it is an expiation. Some scholars mentioned that the night prayer was obligatory upon him at the beginning, then he was permitted to leave it, and so it became supererogatory. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned two opinions in this regard: First, it is close to what Mujahid said: when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed voluntary prayer, it could not be for him a means of erasing sins, since his past and future sins had been forgiven; whereas for others, when they perform voluntary prayer, they hope and expect that the erasure of their evil deeds will come through the voluntary prayer, so the nāfilah for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is an excess beyond need, while for others it is a necessity, and something hoped for to repel what is disliked. Second: the nāfilah is for the Prophet ﷺ and his ummah, and the meaning is: "And from the night, perform tahajjud with it as a supererogatory for you," so the Prophet ﷺ was addressed with the address of his ummah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you﴾: "It may be" (ʿasā) from Allah is obligatory, and the meaning of "will raise you" is: will station you in ﴿a praiseworthy station﴾, which is the one for which all the people of the gathering will praise him. Regarding it there are two opinions: First: that it is the intercession for people on the Day of Resurrection, said by Ibn Masʿud, Huzayfah ibn al-Yaman, Ibn ʿUmar, Salman al-Farisi, Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, and al-Hasan, and it is the narration of Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid. Second: He will seat him upon the Throne on the Day of Resurrection. Abu Wa'il narrated from ʿAbd Allah that he recited this verse and said: "He will seat him upon the Throne," and likewise al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Layth from Mujahid.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance﴾. Al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, al-Dahhak, Humayd ibn Qays, and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read (mudkhala) and (mukhraja) with a fatha on the mim. Al-Zajjaj said: mudkhal with a damma on the mim is the verbal noun of adkhaltuhu mudkhalan; and whoever says mudkhala sidq, it is on the basis of adkhaltuhu, so he entered a sound entrance; and likewise he explained mukhraja similarly.

Regarding the intended meaning of this entrance and exit, the commentators have eleven opinions:

First: "Cause me to enter Medina with a sound entrance, and cause me to exit Mecca with a sound exit." Abu Zabyan narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in Mecca, then he was commanded to emigrate, and this verse was revealed to him." To this meaning went al-Hasan in the narration of Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd.

Second: "Cause me to enter the grave with a sound entrance, and cause me to exit from it with a sound exit," narrated by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Third: "Cause me to enter Medina, and cause me to exit to Mecca," meaning for its conquest, narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Fourth: "Cause me to enter Mecca with a sound entrance, and cause me to exit from it with a sound exit," so he exited from it safe from the polytheists, and entered it openly over them on the day of the conquest, said by al-Dahhak.

Fifth: "Cause me to enter the sound entrance of Paradise, and cause me to exit with a sound exit from Mecca to Medina," narrated by Qatadah from al-Hasan.

Sixth: "Cause me to enter into prophethood and messengership, and cause me to exit from them with a sound exit," said by Mujahid, meaning: cause me to exit from what is obligatory upon me in them.

Seventh: "Cause me to enter into Islam and cause me to exit from it," said by Abu Salih, meaning: from the fulfilment of what is obligatory upon me in it when death comes.

Eighth: "Cause me to enter into Your obedience and cause me to exit from it," i.e., safe, not falling short in performing it, said by ʿAta'.

Ninth: "Cause me to enter the cave and cause me to exit from it," said by Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir.

Tenth: "Cause me to enter into the religion and cause me to exit from the world while I am upon the truth," mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

Eleventh: "Cause me to enter Mecca and cause me to exit to Hunayn," mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

As for the attribution of sidq (sound/truthfulness) to the entrance and the exit, it is a praise of both. We have explained this meaning in Surah Yunus (10:2).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And grant me from Yourself authority (sultan)﴾; i.e., from Your presence. Regarding it there are three opinions: First: that it is dominance over the disbelievers by the sword, and over the hypocrites by establishing the hudud, said by al-Hasan. Second: that it is the clear proof, said by Mujahid. Third: the mighty king by whom the disobedient are subdued, said by Qatadah. Ibn al-Anbari said: His saying "nasīran (a helper)" may be in the sense of munassiran (one who grants victory), and it is suitable that its interpretation be nasiran (helping).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And say: The truth has come and falsehood has vanished﴾. Regarding it there are four opinions: First: that the truth is Islam and the falsehood is shirk, said by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas. Second: that the truth is the Qurʾan and the falsehood is Satan, said by Qatadah. Third: that the truth is jihad and the falsehood is shirk, said by Ibn Jurayj. Fourth: the truth is the worship of God and the falsehood is the worship of idols, said by Muqatil. The meaning of "zahaqa" is: it perished and vanished; everything that is destroyed and annulled has zahaqa, and "zahaqat nafsuhu" means his soul perished.

Ibn Masʿud narrated that "the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered Mecca while around the House were three hundred and sixty idols, and he began striking them and saying: 'The truth has come and falsehood has vanished; indeed falsehood was ever bound to vanish.'"

If it is said: How can you say that "zahaqa" means "batala (was annulled)," while falsehood exists and is acted upon by its adherents?

The answer: what is meant by its annulment and perishing is the clarity of its defect, so that it is perished in the eyes of the one who reflects and looks.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Establish the prayer﴾; i.e., perform it, ﴿at the decline of the sun﴾; i.e., at its declining. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned two opinions regarding the lam (in li-dulūki): first, that it means "in" (fī). Second, that it is emphatic (muʾakkadah), like His saying ﴿It has followed closely upon you﴾ [An-Naml: 72]. Abu ʿUbayda said: its dulūk is from the time of its zawal (passing of the meridian) until it sets. Al-Zajjaj said: its inclination at midday is dulūk, and its inclination toward sunset is dulūk. Al-Azhari said: the meaning of al-dulūk (declining) in the speech of the Arabs is zawal (decline/passing), and for this reason the sun, when it passes the middle of the day, is called dālikah, and when it sets, it is called dālikah, because in both states it is declining.

Regarding the intended meaning of dulūk here, the commentators have two opinions:

First: that it is its zawal at midday. Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah narrated: "I invited the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and whomever of his companions he wished, and they ate at my place. Then they went out when the sun had passed its zenith, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out and said: 'Go out, O Abu Bakr, for this is when the sun declines (dalakat al-shams).'" This is the view of Ibn ʿUmar, Abu Barzah, Abu Hurayrah, al-Hasan, al-Shaʿbi, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Abu al-ʿAliyah, Mujahid, ʿAta', ʿUbayd ibn ʿUmayr, Qatadah, al-Dahhak, and Muqatil, and it is the choice of al-Azhari. Al-Azhari said: so that the verse encompasses the five prayers, the meaning being: "Establish the prayer from the time of the sun's zawal until the darkness of the night (ghasaq al-layl)," which includes the Dhuhr, the ʿAsr, and the two prayers of the darkness of the night, which are the ʿIshaʾs; then He said: ﴿and the Qurʾan of dawn﴾, and so these are five prayers.

Second: that it is its setting. This was said by Ibn Masʿud, al-Nakhaʿi, and Ibn Zayd, and from Ibn ʿAbbas there are two reports similar to the two opinions. Al-Farraʾ said: I have seen the Arabs understand dulūk as the disappearance of the sun, and this is the choice of Ibn Qutaybah. He said: because the Arabs say: "the star declined (dalaka al-najm)" when it set. Dhu al-Rummah said:

Lamps that are not led by the stars (nujūm) nor by the setting ones (al-afilāt al-dawālik)

And they say of the sun: "dalakat bi-rāḥ," meaning it set, while the observer has placed his palm on his brow looking at it. A poet said:

And the sun has nearly become a sick one, / I push it with wine that it may slip away

He likened it to the sick man in his final illness (danaf), because it was about to set, just as death approaches the one in the final illness. The observer looks at it from beneath the palm only to know how much remains for it until it sets, and to shield the rays with his hand. Accordingly, on this view the prayer intended is the Maghrib. As for the darkness of the night (ghasaq al-layl), it is its darkness.

Regarding the intended prayer connected with the darkness of the night, there are three opinions: First: the ʿIshaʾ, said by Ibn Masʿud. Second: the Maghrib, said by Ibn ʿAbbas. Al-Qadi Abu Yaʿla said: it is possible that the intended meaning is clarifying the time of the Maghrib, that it runs from the sun's setting until the darkness of the night. Third: the Maghrib and the ʿIshaʾ, said by al-Hasan.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and the Qurʾan of dawn﴾ means: and establish the recitation of dawn. The commentators said: what is intended by it is the Fajr prayer. Al-Zajjaj said: in this there is a great benefit, indicating that the prayer is not except with recitation, since the prayer has been called "Qurʾan."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the Qurʾan of dawn is ever witnessed﴾. Abu Hurayrah narrated from the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "The angels of the night and the angels of the day witness it."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And from the night, pray Tahajjud with it﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: pray with the Qurʾan. Mujahid, ʿAlqamah, and al-Aswad said: tahajjud is after sleep. Ibn Qutaybah said: tahajjadtu means I stayed awake, and hajadtu means I slept. Ibn al-Anbari said: tahajjud here means alertness and wakefulness, and the lexicographers say it is one of the words with opposite meanings: it is said of the sleeper: hājid and mutahajjid, and likewise of the one who stays awake. al-Nabighah said:

Even if she appeared to a white-haired monk, a servant of God, a celibate, mutahajjid

We would be amazed at her beauty and the sweetness of her speech, and at her mole, though he would not be rightly guided

By al-mutahajjid he means the one who stays awake. Labid said:

He said: "We have slept, for the night has grown long, / and we have been able, if we were heedless of time..."

That is, "he put us to sleep." Al-Azhari said: al-mutahajjid is one who rises from sleep to prayer. It was said of him: mutahajjid, because he casts off drowsiness (hujūd) from himself, just as one says: taharraja and ta'ththama (he avoided sin and acted sinfully).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿as a supererogatory (nāfilah) for you﴾. Nāfilah in the language means what is in excess of the basic obligation.

Regarding the meaning of this excess in his case, there are two opinions:

First: that it is an addition to what was obligated upon him, so the meaning is: an obligation upon you. The qiyam al-layl was obligatory upon him. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

Second: that it is an addition beyond the obligation and is not obligatory; the meaning is: voluntary and virtuous. Abu Umamah, al-Hasan, and Mujahid said: the nāfilah is for the Prophet ﷺ alone. Mujahid said: this is because his past and future sins have been forgiven, so whatever exceeds his obligation is a supererogatory and a virtue for him, while for others it is an expiation. Some scholars mentioned that the night prayer was obligatory upon him at the beginning, then he was permitted to leave it, and so it became supererogatory. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned two opinions in this regard: First, it is close to what Mujahid said: when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed voluntary prayer, it could not be for him a means of erasing sins, since his past and future sins had been forgiven; whereas for others, when they perform voluntary prayer, they hope and expect that the erasure of their evil deeds will come through the voluntary prayer, so the nāfilah for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is an excess beyond need, while for others it is a necessity, and something hoped for to repel what is disliked. Second: the nāfilah is for the Prophet ﷺ and his ummah, and the meaning is: "And from the night, perform tahajjud with it as a supererogatory for you," so the Prophet ﷺ was addressed with the address of his ummah.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you﴾: "It may be" (ʿasā) from Allah is obligatory, and the meaning of "will raise you" is: will station you in ﴿a praiseworthy station﴾, which is the one for which all the people of the gathering will praise him. Regarding it there are two opinions: First: that it is the intercession for people on the Day of Resurrection, said by Ibn Masʿud, Huzayfah ibn al-Yaman, Ibn ʿUmar, Salman al-Farisi, Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, and al-Hasan, and it is the narration of Ibn Abi Najih from Mujahid. Second: He will seat him upon the Throne on the Day of Resurrection. Abu Wa'il narrated from ʿAbd Allah that he recited this verse and said: "He will seat him upon the Throne," and likewise al-Dahhak narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Layth from Mujahid.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance﴾. Al-Hasan, ʿIkrimah, al-Dahhak, Humayd ibn Qays, and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read (mudkhala) and (mukhraja) with a fatha on the mim. Al-Zajjaj said: mudkhal with a damma on the mim is the verbal noun of adkhaltuhu mudkhalan; and whoever says mudkhala sidq, it is on the basis of adkhaltuhu, so he entered a sound entrance; and likewise he explained mukhraja similarly.

First: "Cause me to enter Medina with a sound entrance, and cause me to exit Mecca with a sound exit." Abu Zabyan narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, he said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was in Mecca, then he was commanded to emigrate, and this verse was revealed to him." To this meaning went al-Hasan in the narration of Saʿid ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd.

Second: "Cause me to enter the grave with a sound entrance, and cause me to exit from it with a sound exit," narrated by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Third: "Cause me to enter Medina, and cause me to exit to Mecca," meaning for its conquest, narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Fourth: "Cause me to enter Mecca with a sound entrance, and cause me to exit from it with a sound exit," so he exited from it safe from the polytheists, and entered it openly over them on the day of the conquest, said by al-Dahhak.

Fifth: "Cause me to enter the sound entrance of Paradise, and cause me to exit with a sound exit from Mecca to Medina," narrated by Qatadah from al-Hasan.

Sixth: "Cause me to enter into prophethood and messengership, and cause me to exit from them with a sound exit," said by Mujahid, meaning: cause me to exit from what is obligatory upon me in them.

Seventh: "Cause me to enter into Islam and cause me to exit from it," said by Abu Salih, meaning: from the fulfilment of what is obligatory upon me in it when death comes.

Eighth: "Cause me to enter into Your obedience and cause me to exit from it," i.e., safe, not falling short in performing it, said by ʿAta'.

Ninth: "Cause me to enter the cave and cause me to exit from it," said by Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir.

Tenth: "Cause me to enter into the religion and cause me to exit from the world while I am upon the truth," mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 82:

His saying, Exalted is He: "﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing﴾": the "min" (min, "of") here is for specifying the kind, so the whole Qur'an is a healing. Concerning this healing there are three opinions:

One: it is a healing from misguidance, because of the guidance it contains. The second: it is a healing from sickness, because of the blessing it contains. The third: it is a healing through the clarification of the obligations (fara'id) and rulings (ahkam).

Concerning "mercy" (rahmah) there are two opinions: one of them: it is a blessing (ni'mah). The second: it is the cause of mercy.

His saying, Exalted is He: "﴿And it does not increase the wrongdoers﴾" meaning: the polytheists, "﴿except in loss﴾", because they disbelieve in it and do not benefit from its admonitions, so their loss increases.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 83–84:

Allah's words: ﴿And when We bestow favor upon man﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "Man" here refers to the disbeliever, and what is meant by him is al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. The exegetes (mufassirun) said: this bestowal is abundance of provision and the removal of affliction. ﴿He turns away and distances himself﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Hafs, from 'Asim, recited (ونأى) on the pattern of (نعى), with a fathah on the nun and the hamzah. Ibn 'Amir recited (ناء) like (باع). Al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, from Salim, from Hamzah, recited (وناء) with imalah of the nun and the hamzah. Khallad related from Salim (نُئِيَ) with a fathah on the nun and a kasrah on the hamzah. The meaning: he distanced himself from carrying out the rights of blessings. It was said: he exalted himself and became arrogant. ﴿And when harm touches him﴾; that is, affliction and poverty befall him. ﴿He is despairing﴾; that is, deeply despairing, hopeless, not hoping for the bounty of Allah.

Allah's words: ﴿Say: Each works according to his manner (shakilatihi)﴾. In it there are three opinions:

The first: according to his side (naahiyatihi), said by Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Al-Farra' said: al-shakilah means the side, the way, and the path. I heard some Arabs say: "'Abd al-Malik at that time was on his jadilah, and Ibn al-Zubayr was on his jadilah," meaning: on his side. Abu 'Ubaydah said: according to his side and his disposition (khaliqah). Ibn Qutaybah said: according to his disposition and nature, and it is from the shakl (likeness). It is said: "I am not on my shakl nor my shakilah." Al-Zajjaj said: according to his way and his school of thought.

The second: according to his intention (niyyah), said by al-Hasan and Mu'awiyah ibn Qurrah. Al-Layth said: the shakilah of matters is that which agrees with its doer.

The third: according to his religion, said by Ibn Zayd. The clarification of the meaning: each one works according to his way that accords with his character. So the disbeliever does what resembles his way of turning away at blessings and despairing at hardship, and the believer does what resembles his way of gratitude in ease and patience in affliction, and Allah rewards both groups. Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas that this verse was abrogated by His words: ﴿Then kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 5], but this is nothing (laysa bi-shay').

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 85:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They ask you about the soul.﴾ Regarding the occasion of its revelation there are two accounts:

The first: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by some Jews, and they said: Ask him about the soul. Some of them said: Do not ask him, lest he confront you with what you dislike. Then a group of them came to him and said: O Abu'l-Qasim, what do you say about the soul? He remained silent, and this verse was revealed." This was related by Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: "The Jews said to the Quraysh: Ask Muhammad about three things. If he tells you about two of them and withholds the third, then he is a prophet. Ask him about a group of youths who disappeared, ask him about Dhu'l-Qarnayn, and ask him about the soul. So they asked him about them. He explained to them the matter of the youths in the cave, and he explained to them the story of Dhu'l-Qarnayn, and he withheld the story of the soul, so this verse was revealed." This was narrated by Ata' from Ibn Abbas. (p. 82)

Regarding what is meant by "the soul" here, there are six opinions:

The first: that it is the spirit by which the body is alive. This meaning was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas. People have differed over the reality (mahiyyah) of the soul, and then they differed over whether the spirit is the self (nafs) or whether they are two distinct things; there is no need to mention their disagreement, because there is no proof for any of that. It is rather something they took from medicine and the philosophers. As for the earlier generation (al-salaf), they refrained from this, due to the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Say: The soul is by the command of my Lord.﴾ When they saw that the people asked about the soul and were not answered, and that revelation was still descending while the Messenger was alive, they knew that silence about what one has not encompassed in true knowledge is preferable.

The second: that the soul here means an angel among the angels of enormous form. This was related from Ali (peace be upon him), Ibn Abbas, and Muqatil.

The third: that the ruh is a creation of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, whose forms are like the forms of the children of Adam. This was narrated by Mujahid from Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: that it is Jibril (peace be upon him). This was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The fifth: that it is the Qur'an. This was also related from al-Hasan.

The sixth: that it is Isa ibn Maryam. This was reported by al-Mawardi. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: Allah, exalted is He, has mentioned the ruh in several places in the Qur'an, so my strong opinion is that the transmitters moved its explanation from its proper place to a place that does not suit it, thinking it to be similar, whereas it is only the spirit by which the son of Adam lives. As for His saying: ﴿"From the command of my Lord"﴾; that is, from His affair, which prevents anyone from knowing it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you have been given of knowledge only a little.﴾ Regarding those addressed by this, there are two opinions:

The first: that they are the Jews. This was said by most scholars. (p. 83)

The second: that they are all of creation, whose knowledge is little in comparison to the knowledge of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. This was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

If it is said: How can this verse be reconciled with the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has certainly been given much good﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269]?

The answer: that what people are given of knowledge, although it is much, is little in comparison to the knowledge of Allah.

**The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verses 86–87:**

Allah's words: ﴿And if We willed, We would surely take away that which We have revealed to you﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: If We willed, We would erase it from the hearts and the books, until no trace of it could be found, ﴿then you would not find for yourself any guardian against Us in regard to it﴾; that is, you would not find anyone who would take up the task (yatawakkalu) of returning any of it. ﴿Except as a mercy from your Lord﴾: this is an exception that is not from the first part. The meaning is: But Allah has shown you mercy, so He established that in your heart and in the hearts of the believers.

Ibn al-Anbari said: The meaning is: But a mercy from your Lord prevents Him from stripping away the Qur'an. The polytheists had addressed their wives among the Muslims, urging them to return to the religion of their fathers, so Allah, Mighty and Majestic, threatened them with the removal of the blessing. The apparent address is to the Messenger, while the meaning of the threat is directed at the community.

Abu Sulayman said: ﴿Then you would not find for yourself against it﴾, that is, against what We do to you by taking away what you have, ﴿a guardian﴾ who would repel Us from what We intend for you.

It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that he said: The Qur'an will be lifted in a single night. Jibril will come in the middle of the night and take it away from their breasts and from their houses, and in the morning they will not recite a single verse (p-84) nor have any awareness of it.

Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi rejected the authenticity of this hadith, citing the Prophet's words (peace and blessings be upon him): "Indeed Allah does not take away knowledge by snatching it." However, the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud is narrated through sound chains. It is possible that the Prophet (ﷺ) meant by "knowledge" that which is other than the Qur'an, for knowledge continues to diminish until the lifting of the Qur'an comes at the very end of time.

Allah says: ﴿Say: "If mankind and the jinn were to gather together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like, even if they were to help one another."﴾

The exegetes said: This is a refutation of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith (al-Nadr ibn al-Harith) when he said: "If we wished, we would say the like of this." The "like" that was demanded of them was speech having a composition like the composition of the Qur'an, at the highest levels of eloquence (balaghah, the science of eloquence). Al-zahir (al-zahir): the helper.

(p-85)

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 89–93:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly diversified for the people in this Qur'an⁠—﴾ We have explained it in this surah [al-Isra': 41]. The meaning is: from every kind of example through which there is a lesson (i'tibar), ﴿but most of the people refused except disbelief﴾, meaning the people of Makkah, ﴿except denial﴾; that is, obstinate rejection of the truth and denial of it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they said, "We will not believe you until you cause to gush forth for us from the earth a spring"﴾. The occasion of revelation of this verse and what follows it: "The leaders of Quraysh, such as 'Utbah, Shaybah, Abu Jahl, 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah, and al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, along with others, gathered at the Ka'bah. Some of them said to others: 'Send to Muhammad and speak with him and argue with him, so that you may be excused regarding him.' So they sent to him that the nobles of your people have gathered to speak with you. He came quickly, for he was eager for their guidance. They said: 'O Muhammad, by God, we know of no man among the Arabs who has brought upon his people what you have brought upon yours. You have reviled the forefathers, disparaged the religion, insulted the forbearance (of people), and divided the community. If you came with this seeking wealth, we will make for you from our wealth so that you will be the richest of us. If you seek nobility among us, we will make you our chief. If this jinn that comes to you has overpowered you, we will spend our wealth seeking a physician for you until we cure you of it or are excused regarding you.' The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'If you accept from me what I have brought you, it is your share in this world and the Hereafter. If you reject it from me, I will be patient with the command of God until God judges between me and you.' They said: 'O Muhammad, if you will not accept from us what we have offered, then you know that there is no one among the people whose lands are more confined or whose life is harder than ours. Ask your Lord to move these mountains away from us that have constricted us, and to make rivers flow for us, and to raise up those of our fathers who have passed away—let Qusayy ibn Kilab be among those raised for us, for he was an elderly truthful man—so that we may ask them about what you say: is it true? If you do this, we will believe you.' The Messenger of God ﷺ said: 'I was not sent with this; I have conveyed to you what I was sent with.' They said: 'Then ask your Lord to send an angel to confirm you, and ask Him to give you gardens, treasures, and palaces of gold and silver that will make you independent.' He said: 'I am not one who asks his Lord for this.' They said: 'Then make the sky fall upon us as you claim, that your Lord will do so if He wills.' He said: 'That is up to God, mighty and majestic.' One of them said: 'We will not believe you until you bring God and the angels before us as a group (qabilan).' 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah said: 'I will not believe you until you take a ladder to the sky and climb up on it while I watch, and bring a written book with you, and a group of angels to bear witness for you.' The Messenger of God ﷺ left, grieved by what he saw of their aversion to him. So God revealed: ﴿And they said, 'We will not believe you...'﴾, the verses." Narrated by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until you cause to gush forth﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, and Ibn 'Amir read: (tafjura) with a dammah on the ta', a fathah on the fa', and a shaddah on the jim with a kasrah. 'Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read: (tafjura) with a fathah on the ta', a sukun on the fa', and a dammah on the jim with lightening (takhfif). The one who reads with the shaddah intends the frequency of gushing from the spring (yanbu'), and the one who reads with the lightened form does so because the spring is singular. As for al-yanbu', it is a spring from which water wells up. Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is a form of yafu'ul, from naba' al-ma', meaning it appeared and gushed forth.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or you have a garden﴾, that is, an orchard, ﴿and you cause rivers to gush forth within it﴾, that is, you open them and make them flow, ﴿amid it﴾, that is, in the middle of that garden.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or you cause the sky to fall upon us﴾. Mujahid, Abu Mijlaz, Abu Raja', Humayd, and al-Jahdari read: (aw tasqut) with a fathah on the ta' and a raf' on the qaf, with "al-sama'" in the nominative.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿in pieces (kisafan)﴾. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read (kisfan) with a sukun on the sin throughout the Qur'an, except in (al-Rum: 48), where they vocalize the sin. Nafi' and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read with vocalization of the sin in both places, and with sukun elsewhere in the Qur'an. Ibn 'Amir reads here with a fathah on the sin, and elsewhere in the Qur'an with a sukun. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads (kisafan) with a fathah on the sin makes it the plural of kisfah, which is a piece. Whoever reads (kisfan) with a sukun on the sin, it is as if they said: make it fall on us as a single covering layer; its derivation is from kasafta al-shay', when you covered it, meaning: make it fall upon us as one piece. Ibn al-Anbari said: whoever reads with sukun says its interpretation is covering and concealment, from the saying "the sun has been eclipsed (inkasafat)" when something intervenes between the viewers and its light.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿or you bring God and the angels as a group (qabilan)﴾. On this there are three views:

First: face to face (i'anan), narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, and said by Qatadah, Ibn Jurayj, and Muqatil. Abu 'Ubaydah said its meaning is confrontation (muqabalah), that is, direct observation, and he recited for al-A'sha:

"We make peace with you until you return with its like, like the cry of a pregnant woman whose group (qabiluha) has eased her."

(p-88)

That is, she faced it. It is also narrated as "wajjahat" (directed it), meaning instead of "yassarat."

Second: a guarantor (kafilan) that you are the Messenger of God, said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and preferred by al-Farra', who said: al-qabil, al-kafil, and al-za'im are the same; one says qabiltu, kafaltu, and za'amtu.

Third: a tribe for each tribe, each on its own, said by al-Hasan and Mujahid.

As for "al-zukhruf," it means gold. We have explained the root of this word in (Yunus: 24). And "tarqa" means ascends; one says raqiitu arqa ruqiyyan.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿until you send down upon us a book﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: a book from the Lord of the worlds addressed to so-and-so son of so-and-so, which each of us reads in the morning.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "Glory be to my Lord"﴾. Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read (qul). Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read (qala), and likewise it is in the codices of the people of Makkah and Syria. ﴿Am I anything but a human messenger?﴾ That is: these things are not within the capacity of humans.

If it is said: why did He limit Himself to relating (qalu) without clarifying the response?

The answer: when He singled them out with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "If mankind and the jinn gathered to produce the like of this Qur'an..."﴾, and they were unable to do so, He rendered them incapable. It is as if He says: I have already made clear to you, through the signs that preceded, what indicates my prophethood, and among that is the challenge with the like of this Qur'an. As for your demands, they are not within my power. Also, they insisted upon him regarding these matters, and did not ask him to ask his Lord, so He answered their claim by his being a human, and that suffices as a response.

(p-٩٠) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever Allah guides, he is the one guided﴾. Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read the yā' (the final ya) when connected, and omitted it in pause. Ya'qub kept it in pause, and most readers omitted it in both states. ﴿Whoever Allah guides﴾: Ibn 'Abbas said, "Whoever Allah wills guidance for." ﴿…and whoever He leads astray, you will not find for them protectors besides Him﴾: they will lead them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We will gather them on the Day of Resurrection upon their faces﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions:

First: He will make them walk upon their faces. Its evidence is what al-Bukhari and Muslim narrated in their two Sahihs, from Anas ibn Malik, that a man asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "How will the disbeliever be gathered upon his face on the Day of Resurrection?" He said: "The One who made him walk on his feet in this world is able to make him walk upon his face on the Day of Resurrection."

Second: The meaning is: We will gather them dragged upon their faces. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Third: We will gather them hastening and rushing. He expressed by His saying ﴿upon their faces﴾ the meaning of haste, as the Arabs say, "The people passed upon their faces," when they hurried. This was said by Ibn al-Anbari.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Blind, dumb, and deaf﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

One: Blind, not seeing anything that would please them; dumb, not speaking any proof; and deaf, not hearing anything that would please them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. In another narration he said: blind from looking at what has been prepared for His friends; dumb from addressing Allah; and deaf to what He praised His friends with. This is the saying of most scholars.

Second: This gathering occurs in some states of the Resurrection after the first gathering. Muqatil said: This happens when it is said to them, ﴿Be driven away therein﴾ (Al-Mu'minun 23:108), and they become blind, dumb, and deaf, neither seeing, nor hearing, nor speaking after that.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whenever it subsides﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: That is, it calms down. The commentators said: That is because it consumes them; when it leaves nothing of them and they become charcoal, and it finds nothing left to consume, (p-٩١) it subsides. Then they are returned to a new creation, and the fire returns to them. Ibn Qutayba said: It is said, "The fire subsided" (khabat al-nar) when its flame calmed. The flame subsides while the ember still works. If the flame subsides and the ember is not extinguished, it is said khamadat, takhmudu, khumudan. If it is extinguished and nothing of it remains, it is said hamadat, tahmudu, humudan. The meaning of ﴿We increase them in blaze﴾ is: a fire that is kindled fiercely, that is, flaring.

As for what follows, its explanation has already been given (Al-Isra 17:49), up to His saying, ﴿Able to create the likes of them﴾; that is, able to create them a second time. By "the likes of them" He meant themselves. The likeness of a thing is equal to it, so it is permissible to express by it the very thing itself. It is said, "One like you does not do this," meaning "you." A similar usage is His saying: ﴿And if they believe in the like of what you have believed﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:137). The speech is complete at His saying "the likes of them." Then He said: ﴿And He has appointed for them a term about which there is no doubt﴾, meaning the term of resurrection. ﴿But the wrongdoers refused except denial﴾: that is, denial of that term.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: "If you possessed the treasuries of my Lord's mercy…"﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: "If you yourselves possessed," as al-Mutalammis said:

Even if other than my maternal uncles wished to harm me,
I would set against them a brand above the nostrils.

The meaning: if other than my maternal uncles had wished…

Concerning these treasuries there are two opinions:

One: the treasuries of provisions. Second: the treasuries of blessings. Accordingly, concerning mercy there are two views: one, provision; the other, blessing. The clarification of the statement is: If you possessed what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, possesses, you would withhold from spending out of fear of poverty. ﴿And man has always been﴾ meaning the disbeliever, ﴿stingy﴾: that is, miserly and withholding. It is said: qatara yaqturu and qatara yaqtiru, when one falls short in spending. Al-Mawardi said: If any of the created beings possessed from the treasuries of Allah, Exalted is He, he would not be as generous as the generosity of Allah, Exalted is He, for two reasons: first, he must retain some of it for his own sustenance and benefit; second, he fears poverty. Allah, Exalted is He, is far above both states in His generosity.

Then Allah, Exalted, mentioned Pharaoh's denial of the signs of Musa, as a comparison to the state of these polytheists, and He said: ﴿And We had certainly given Musa nine clear signs﴾. Concerning them there are two opinions:

The first: they are his tongue and the sea that was split for him. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, meaning by his tongue that there was a knot in it which Allah, Exalted, loosened for him. The second: the sea and the mountain which was lifted over them, narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. The third: the years of drought and the decrease of fruits, narrated by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas; Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, 'Ikrimah, and Qatadah also said this. al-Hasan said: the years of drought and the decrease of fruits are one sign. The fourth: the sea and death, which was sent upon them; said by al-Hasan and Wahb. The fifth: the stone and the sea; said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The sixth: his tongue and the throwing of the staff twice before Pharaoh; said by al-Dahhak. The seventh: the sea and the years of drought; said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b. The eighth: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b also, mentioning the first seven signs, except that in place of his hand he put the sea, and he added the effacement and the stone, meaning His saying: ﴿Efface their wealth﴾ (Yunus 10:88).

It is said, "One like you does not do this," meaning "you." A similar usage is His saying: ﴿And if they believe in the like of what you have believed﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:137). The speech is complete at His saying "the likes of them." Then He said: ﴿And He has appointed for them a term about which there is no doubt﴾, meaning the term of resurrection. ﴿But the wrongdoers refused except denial﴾: that is, denial of that term.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: "If you possessed the treasuries of my Lord's mercy…"﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: "If you yourselves possessed," as al-Mutalammis said:

Even if other than my maternal uncles wished to harm me,
I would set against them a brand above the nostrils.

The meaning: if other than my maternal uncles had wished…

Concerning these treasuries there are two opinions:

One: the treasuries of provisions. Second: the treasuries of blessings. Accordingly, concerning mercy there are two views: one, provision; the other, blessing. The clarification of the statement is: If you possessed what Allah, Mighty and Majestic, possesses, you would withhold from spending out of fear of poverty. ﴿And man has always been﴾ meaning the disbeliever, ﴿stingy﴾: that is, miserly and withholding. It is said: qatara yaqturu and qatara yaqtiru, when one falls short in spending. Al-Mawardi said: If any of the created beings possessed from the treasuries of Allah, Exalted is He, he would not be as generous as the generosity of Allah, Exalted is He, for two reasons: first, he must retain some of it for his own sustenance and benefit; second, he fears poverty. Allah, Exalted is He, is far above both states in His generosity.

Then Allah, Exalted, mentioned Pharaoh's denial of the signs of Musa, as a comparison to the state of these polytheists, and He said: ﴿And We had certainly given Musa nine clear signs﴾. Concerning them there are two opinions:

One: they are the miracles and proofs. Then the majority of commentators agreed upon seven of them: his hand, the staff, the flood, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, and the blood. They differed about the last two on eight opinions:

The first: they are his tongue and the sea that was split for him. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, meaning by his tongue that there was a knot in it which Allah, Exalted, loosened for him. The second: the sea and the mountain which was lifted over them, narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. The third: the years of drought and the decrease of fruits, narrated by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas; Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, 'Ikrimah, and Qatadah also said this. al-Hasan said: the years of drought and the decrease of fruits are one sign. The fourth: the sea and death, which was sent upon them; said by al-Hasan and Wahb. The fifth: the stone and the sea; said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The sixth: his tongue and the throwing of the staff twice before Pharaoh; said by al-Dahhak. The seventh: the sea and the years of drought; said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b. The eighth: Muhammad ibn Ishaq narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b also, mentioning the first seven signs, except that in place of his hand he put the sea, and he added the effacement and the stone, meaning His saying: ﴿Efface their wealth﴾ (Yunus 10:88).

Second: they are the verses of the Book. Abu Dawud al-Sijistani narrated from the hadith of Safwan ibn 'Assal, that a Jew said to his companion: "Come, let us ask this Prophet." The other said: "Do not say he is a prophet, for if he hears that, he will have four eyes." So they came to him and asked him about nine clear signs. He said: "Do not associate anything with Allah; do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right; (p-٩٣) do not commit adultery; do not steal; do not consume usury; do not bring the innocent to the ruler to have him killed; do not practise sorcery; do not slander chaste women; do not flee from the battlefield; and especially upon you, O Jews, do not transgress on the Sabbath." He said: So they kissed his hand and said: "We testify that you are a prophet."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verses 101–104:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So ask the Children of Israel﴾. The majority of readers recited "fa-s'al" (so ask) as an imperative addressed to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). He was commanded to ask those among them who had believed about what he had reported concerning them, so that it would be a proof against those among them who did not believe. Ibn ʿAbbas recited "fa-saʾala Banī Isrāʾīl" (so he [Moses] asked the Children of Israel), in the sense of a report about Moses, that he asked Pharaoh to send the Children of Israel with him. ﴿Pharaoh said to him: "Indeed, I think you, O Moses, are bewitched"﴾; that is, "I surely suppose you," ﴿O Moses, bewitched﴾. On the meaning of "maswūran" (bewitched) there are three opinions:

The first: deceived. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: "bewitched," meaning you have been enchanted. This was said by Ibn al-Sāʾib. The third: "sāḥiran" (a sorcerer), where the passive participle is placed in the position of the active participle. This is reported from al-Farrāʾ and Abū ʿUbayda. Moses said: ﴿Certainly you know﴾. The majority recited it with a fatḥa on the tāʾ. ʿAlī (peace be upon him) recited it with a ḍamma, and said: "By Allah, the enemy of Allah did not know, but it was Moses who knew." This reached Ibn ʿAbbas, who argued with the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them﴾ [an-Naml 27:14]. Al-Kisāʾī and Thaʿlab preferred the reading of ʿAlī (peace be upon him), and it has been reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, Abū Razīn, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, and Ibn Yaʿmar. Those who supported it argued that when Moses was accused of being bewitched, he was informed of the soundness of his reason by the saying: "Certainly you know." But the first reading is more correct, because of the choice of the majority, and because Moses had shown from the miracles what compelled Pharaoh's knowledge of his truthfulness, so Pharaoh did not respond to him except with excuses and evasion. It is as if he had said: "Certainly you know, by the proof and the evidence," ﴿that none sent down these except the Lord of the heavens and the earth as clear evidence﴾, meaning: the signs. We have explained the meaning of "baṣāʾir" (clear evidence) in (al-Aʿrāf 7:203).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are lost﴾. Most of the exegetes said: "al-ẓann" (thinking) here means knowledge, in contrast to Pharaoh's thinking about Moses. Some of them equated the two, making the first also mean knowledge.

On "mathbūr" (lost, destroyed) there are six opinions:

The first: that it means accursed. This was reported by Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk also said so. The second: defeated; reported by al-ʿAwfī from Ibn ʿAbbas. The third: deficient in intellect; reported by Maymūn ibn Mihrān from Ibn ʿAbbas. The fourth: destroyed; reported by Ibn Abī Ṭalḥa from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abū ʿUbayda and Ibn Qutayba also said so. al-Zajjāj said: "It is said: thabara al-rajul, so he is mathbūr, when he is destroyed." The fifth: perishing; said by Mujāhid. The sixth: prevented from good; the Arabs say: "mā thabaraka ʿan hādhā," meaning: what prevented you from this? This was said by al-Farrāʾ.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So he intended to scare them out of the land﴾. That is, Pharaoh intended to drive the Children of Israel out of the land of Egypt. Regarding the meaning of ﴿yastafizzahum﴾ (to scare them) there are two opinions:

One: he would uproot them; said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: he would make them light (in importance) until they leave; said by Ibn Qutayba. al-Zajjāj said: It is possible that their being scared out means expelling them from it by killing or by removal. The scholars said: In this verse there is an indication of the support of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because when Moses left and Pharaoh pursued him, Pharaoh was destroyed and Moses took possession. Likewise Allah made His Prophet victorious after his departure from Makkah, until he returned to it as a dominant ruler over it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We said after him﴾; that is, after the destruction of Pharaoh, ﴿to the Children of Israel: "Dwell in the land."﴾ On which land there are three opinions:

The first: Palestine and Jordan; said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: a land beyond China; said by Muqātil. The third: the land of Egypt and Syria.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We will bring you together as a mixed multitude﴾; that is, all together. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujāhid, and Ibn Qutayba. al-Farrāʾ said: "laffīfan" means from here and from here. al-Zajjāj said: "al-laffīf" means groups from various tribes.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verse 105–109:

Allah's statement: ﴿And with the truth We have sent it down﴾. The pronoun "hu" (it) refers to the Qur'an. The meaning: We sent down the Qur'an with the established command and the upright religion, so it is true, its descent is true, and what it contains is true. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: ﴿And with the truth We have sent it down﴾, i.e., with monotheism (tawhid); ﴿and with the truth it descended﴾, meaning: with the promise and the warning, and the command and the prohibition.

Allah's statement: ﴿And a Qur'an We have divided﴾. Ali (peace be upon him), Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, Ubayy ibn Ka'b, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Abu Razin, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, Qatadah, al-A'raj, Abu Raja', and Ibn Muhaysin read ( farraqnahu ) with the doubled letter (tashdid), while the majority (al-Jumhur) read it without doubling (takhfif).

As for the reading with the single letter, there are three opinions regarding its meaning:

One: We made its lawful and unlawful clear. This was narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas.

The second: We distinguished within it between truth and falsehood. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: We made it firm and detailed, like His statement: ﴿In it every wise matter is made distinct﴾ [al-Dukhan: 4]. This was said by al-Farra'.

As for the doubled reading, its meaning is that it was sent down in parts, and was not sent down all at once. We have already explained at the beginning of this book the length of the period during which it was revealed. (p-97)

Allah's statement: ﴿So that you may recite it to the people at a slow pace﴾. Anas, al-Sha'bi, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, Abu Raja', Aban from Asim, and Ibn Muhaysin read ( makth ) with a fatha on the mim, and the meaning is: with deliberation and measured recitation, so that they may reflect upon its meaning.

Allah's statement: ﴿Say: Believe in it or do not believe﴾. This is a threat to the disbelievers [of the people of] Makkah, and the pronoun refers to the Qur'an. ﴿Indeed, those who were given knowledge﴾. Regarding them there are three opinions:

One: They are people from the People of the Book, said by Mujahid.

The second: They are the Prophets (peace be upon them), said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: They are seekers of the religion, such as Abu Dharr, Salman, Waraqah ibn Nawfal, and Zayd ibn Amr, said by al-Wahidi.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 17, verses 110–111:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Gracious (ar-Rahman)...﴾ [the verse]. This verse was revealed concerning two occasions. The first part, up to His saying ﴿the Most Beautiful names﴾, was revealed concerning one occasion, and regarding it there are three opinions:

One of them: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ performed the night prayer (tahajjud) one night in Makkah, and in his prostration he began to say: 'O Most Gracious, O Most Merciful.' The polytheists said: 'Muhammad used to call upon one God, but now he calls upon two gods: Allah and the Most Gracious. We do not know the Most Gracious except the Most Gracious of al-Yamamah,' meaning Musaylimah. So Allah revealed this verse." This was related by Ibn Abbas.

The second: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to write at the beginning of what was revealed to him: 'In Your name, O Allah,' until there was revealed: ﴿Indeed it is from Solomon, and indeed it is: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ [an-Naml 27:30]. So he wrote: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.' The polytheists of the Arabs said: 'This Most Merciful we know, but what is the Most Gracious?' So this verse was revealed." This was said by Maymun ibn Mihran.

The third: that the People of the Book said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "You mention the Most Gracious very little, while Allah has mentioned this name abundantly in the Torah." So this verse was revealed. This was said by ad-Dahhak.

As for His saying: ﴿And do not be loud in your prayer﴾, it was revealed concerning one occasion, and regarding it there are three opinions:

One of them: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to raise his voice with the Qur'an in Makkah, and the polytheists would revile the Qur'an and the one who brought it. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ lowered his voice afterward until he was not making his companions hear. So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And do not be loud in your prayer﴾, meaning in your recitation, lest the polytheists hear and revile the Qur'an, ﴿nor be silent in it﴾, regarding your companions, so that they do not hear." This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: that a Bedouin used to speak loudly and raise his voice during the tashahhud, so this verse was revealed. This is the saying of Aisha.

The third: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to pray in Makkah at as-Safa, and he recited the Qur'an aloud in the dawn prayer. Abu Jahl said: 'Do not slander Allah.' So the Prophet ﷺ lowered his voice. Abu Jahl then said to the polytheists: 'Do you not see what I did to the son of Abu Kabshah? I turned him back from his recitation.' So this verse was revealed." This was said by Muqatil.

As for the interpretation: His saying ﴿Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Gracious﴾ means: if you wish, say "O Allah," and if you wish, say "O Most Gracious," for both refer to one [Being]. ﴿Whichever you call﴾ means: whichever of Allah's names you call upon. Al-Farra' said: "ma" may be a superfluous particle (silah), as in His saying ﴿In a little while they will surely become regretful﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:40], and it may carry the meaning of "ayy" (whichever), repeated because their wording differs.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not be loud in your prayer﴾ has two opinions:

One of them: that it refers to the legislated prayer. Then, regarding the meaning of the speech, there are six opinions:

The first: "Do not be loud in your recitation, nor be silent in it," as if He forbade extreme loudness in recitation and extreme quietness. This was said by Ibn Abbas. According to this, regarding calling recitation "prayer," there are two views mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari: one, that the meaning is "do not be loud in the recitation of your prayer"; and two, that recitation is a part of the prayer, so it stands in for it, just as Jesus was called "the Word of Allah," because he came into being by the Word.

The second: "Do not pray to be seen by people, nor abandon it out of fear of people." This was also said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: "Do not be loud in the tashahhud in your prayer." It was narrated from Aisha in one narration, and Ibn Sirin said this as well.

The fourth: "Do not be loud in the outward performance of your prayer, nor be extremely hidden in it." This was said by Ikrimah.

The fifth: "Do not beautify its outward appearance while corrupting its inward state." This was said by al-Hasan.

The sixth: "Do not be loud in all of your prayer, nor be silent in all of it. Be loud in the night prayer and quiet in the day prayer, as We have commanded you." This was mentioned by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la.

The second opinion: that the intended "prayer" is supplication (du'a'). This is the view of Aisha, Abu Hurairah, and Mujahid.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nor be silent in it﴾ — al-mukhafatah means concealment; it is said: "a faint (khafit) voice." ﴿And seek between that a way﴾ means: take a path between loudness and quietness. It has been narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "This verse was abrogated by His saying: ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and with fear, and below the level of loud speech﴾ [al-A'raf 7:205]." Ibn as-Sa'ib said: "It was abrogated by His saying: ﴿So proclaim what you are commanded﴾ [al-Hijr 15:94]." However, on careful examination, the existence of abrogation here is far-fetched.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He has no partner in the dominion﴾. Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu al-Jawza', and Talhah ibn Musarrif read "fi al-milk" with a kasra on the mim. ﴿And He has no protector out of weakness﴾. Mujahid said: "He has not allied with anyone, nor sought anyone's help." The meaning is that He has no need for allegiance to anyone to remedy a humiliation that befalls Him; He is free of needing a protector or helper. ﴿And magnify Him with full magnification﴾, i.e., exalt Him with complete exaltation.

We do not know the Most Gracious except the Most Gracious of al-Yamamah,' meaning Musaylimah. So Allah revealed this verse." This was related by Ibn Abbas.

The second: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to write at the beginning of what was revealed to him: 'In Your name, O Allah,' until there was revealed: ﴿Indeed it is from Solomon, and indeed it is: In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful﴾ [an-Naml 27:30]. So he wrote: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.' The polytheists of the Arabs said: 'This Most Merciful we know, but what is the Most Gracious?' So this verse was revealed." This was said by Maymun ibn Mihran.

The third: that the People of the Book said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "You mention the Most Gracious very little, while Allah has mentioned this name abundantly in the Torah." So this verse was revealed. This was said by ad-Dahhak.

As for His saying: ﴿And do not be loud in your prayer﴾, it was revealed concerning one occasion, and regarding it there are three opinions:

One of them: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to raise his voice with the Qur'an in Makkah, and the polytheists would revile the Qur'an and the one who brought it. So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ lowered his voice afterward until he was not making his companions hear. So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And do not be loud in your prayer﴾, meaning in your recitation, lest the polytheists hear and revile the Qur'an, ﴿nor be silent in it﴾, regarding your companions, so that they do not hear." This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: that a Bedouin used to speak loudly and raise his voice during the tashahhud, so this verse was revealed. This is the saying of Aisha.

The third: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to pray in Makkah at as-Safa, and he recited the Qur'an aloud in the dawn prayer. Abu Jahl said: 'Do not slander Allah.' So the Prophet ﷺ lowered his voice. Abu Jahl then said to the polytheists: 'Do you not see what I did to the son of Abu Kabshah? I turned him back from his recitation.' So this verse was revealed." This was said by Muqatil.

As for the interpretation: His saying ﴿Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Gracious﴾ means: if you wish, say "O Allah," and if you wish, say "O Most Gracious," for both refer to one [Being]. ﴿Whichever you call﴾ means: whichever of Allah's names you call upon. Al-Farra' said: "ma" may be a superfluous particle (silah), as in His saying ﴿In a little while they will surely become regretful﴾ [al-Mu'minun 23:40], and it may carry the meaning of "ayy" (whichever), repeated because their wording differs.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not be loud in your prayer﴾ has two opinions:

One of them: that it refers to the legislated prayer. Then, regarding the meaning of the speech, there are six opinions:

The first: "Do not be loud in your recitation, nor be silent in it," as if He forbade extreme loudness in recitation and extreme quietness. This was said by Ibn Abbas. According to this, regarding calling recitation "prayer," there are two views mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari: one, that the meaning is "do not be loud in the recitation of your prayer"; and two, that recitation is a part of the prayer, so it stands in for it, just as Jesus was called "the Word of Allah," because he came into being by the Word.

The second: "Do not pray to be seen by people, nor abandon it out of fear of people." This was also said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: "Do not be loud in the tashahhud in your prayer." It was narrated from Aisha in one narration, and Ibn Sirin said this as well.

The fourth: "Do not be loud in the outward performance of your prayer, nor be extremely hidden in it." This was said by Ikrimah.

The fifth: "Do not beautify its outward appearance while corrupting its inward state." This was said by al-Hasan.

The sixth: "Do not be loud in all of your prayer, nor be silent in all of it. Be loud in the night prayer and quiet in the day prayer, as We have commanded you." This was mentioned by al-Qadi Abu Ya'la.

The second opinion: that the intended "prayer" is supplication (du'a'). This is the view of Aisha, Abu Hurairah, and Mujahid.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Nor be silent in it﴾ — al-mukhafatah means concealment; it is said: "a faint (khafit) voice." ﴿And seek between that a way﴾ means: take a path between loudness and quietness. It has been narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "This verse was abrogated by His saying: ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and with fear, and below the level of loud speech﴾ [al-A'raf 7:205]." Ibn as-Sa'ib said: "It was abrogated by His saying: ﴿So proclaim what you are commanded﴾ [al-Hijr 15:94]." However, on careful examination, the existence of abrogation here is far-fetched.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He has no partner in the dominion﴾. Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu al-Jawza', and Talhah ibn Musarrif read "fi al-milk" with a kasra on the mim. ﴿And He has no protector out of weakness﴾. Mujahid said: "He has not allied with anyone, nor sought anyone's help." The meaning is that He has no need for allegiance to anyone to remedy a humiliation that befalls Him; He is free of needing a protector or helper. ﴿And magnify Him with full magnification﴾, i.e., exalt Him with complete exaltation.
